prompt: Imagine a dusty VHS tape picked up at a forgotten thrift shop that, whenever watched by anyone born after 1990, implants vivid false memories of an alternate childhood. Explore themes of nostalgia distorted by anomaly and the moral dilemmas of containing such a cognitohazard. Include detailed containment procedures, at least one breach incident log, and testimonies from affected subjects.

outline.name: Three Dollars
outline.description: Archivist Mara Venn surveys the collapsing stock of a rural Pennsylvania thrift shop while reflecting on her distrust of nostalgia and her father's final obsession with a nonexistent daughter named Ruth. Beneath obsolete exercise tapes, she finds a swollen VHS cassette labeled HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. The shopkeeper cannot remember its source. Mara buys it for three dollars, intending to clean and catalog it, unaware that the tape has already begun its next circulation.

outline.name: The Yellow House
outline.description: Back at Mara's archive, assistant Daniel Reyes repairs an old television and loads the tape before Mara can inspect it. The footage shows a yellow-sided house, a woman in a red bathing suit, a plastic pool, and two children running through a sprinkler. Daniel recognizes the smaller child as himself. He describes details not visible in the footage, including a basement window, a dog named Pickle, and a sister called Lily.

outline.name: Lily
outline.description: Daniel's supposed memories arrive with sensory force: swimming lessons, thunderstorms, arguments with Lily, and a lullaby sung by his mother Elena. Mara verifies that Daniel was raised as an only child in New Jersey by a living mother named Elena who never owned the yellow house. Daniel remains euphoric, claiming the tape restored a stolen portion of his life. Mara notices that he is not merely inventing details; he is grieving someone he has never met.

outline.name: The Photograph
outline.description: Daniel's mother denies the existence of Lily and the yellow house during a tense video call, but briefly asks whether Lily is still there before hanging up in terror. Daniel discovers a birthday card addressed to Danny and Lily. A photograph in his apartment changes from an image of him outside a brick building into a picture of two children beside the yellow house. Mara realizes the anomaly can alter records and relationships, not just individual recollection.

outline.name: A Memory of Ruth
outline.description: Mara attempts to destroy the cassette in an industrial shredder and then in a film furnace, but both efforts fail. While handling it, she experiences a brief, emotionally overwhelming memory of standing in a hallway beside a child with a chipped front tooth. She knows the scene is impossible, yet feels genuine grief when it vanishes. Daniel becomes angry when Mara calls Lily unreal, and the Department of Anomalous Media arrives before Mara can file a normal incident report.

outline.name: AM-97-441
outline.description: Department agents seize the tape, quarantine the archive, and identify it as AM-97-441, a post-1990 cognitohazard. They explain that people born after January 1, 1991, are vulnerable to autobiographical implantation, while older viewers may experience emotional bleed-through. Daniel is taken into custody for observation. Mara is offered a nondisclosure agreement or monitored consultant status and accepts the latter after learning that the department has tracked the tape through multiple owners.

outline.name: The Paper Mill
outline.description: Mara is transported to a converted paper mill in rural Pennsylvania, where anomalous media are contained. She sees the restricted vault: lightless, ceramic-lined, copper-meshed, and isolated from digital systems. Agents explain that the tape is kept in a triple-sealed canister inside a suspension locker. Daniel is held in a supervised medical wing, separated from his possessions and family while his memories continue to intensify.

outline.name: Rules for Looking
outline.description: Mara receives the formal containment procedures. Only personnel born before the cutoff may enter the vault; every worker undergoes biometric verification, blood oxygen testing, and spoken identity checks before and after contact. Playback is performed remotely by a mechanical arm through an analog deck with no recording head. Three operators must simultaneously sever the signal. No cameras, wireless devices, magnetic storage, or unapproved descriptions are permitted.

outline.name: The Interview Schedule
outline.description: The department explains its exposure protocol: sedation, isolation, removal of personal objects, and interviews within six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days. Unauthorized copies, transcripts, sketches, recordings, and descriptive notes are destroyed because context may help reconstruct the anomaly. Mara objects that destroying testimony prevents understanding, but Dr. Irena Vale argues that a description carrying emotional detail may be as dangerous as an image.

outline.name: The Lakeside Camp
outline.description: Mara reviews redacted testimonies from earlier cases. A woman born in 1992 remembers an idyllic lakeside camp with a grandmother who died before her birth and begs to return there. The testimony shows that the tape creates a childhood around emotional deprivation rather than replaying a fixed film. Mara is disturbed by how the subject's false memories are factually impossible but emotionally coherent, complete with smells, weather, and private jokes.

outline.name: The Pantry
outline.description: Another testimony concerns a man raised in foster care who remembers loving parents hiding him in a pantry during a tornado. Convinced his foster mother stole him from his true family, he attacks her. The department's clinical notes describe his original memories as technically accessible but emotionally hollow. Mara sees the danger of treating false nostalgia as harmless comfort and begins questioning whether containment can ethically require people to surrender feelings that have become part of their identities.

outline.name: Daniel's Second Childhood
outline.description: Daniel's first formal interviews reveal a detailed alternate life: Elena's red bathing suit, Lily's chipped tooth, a brown dog, swimming lessons, and a birthday party on a cracked ceramic plate. He can still recite facts about his real upbringing but speaks of them with embarrassment and contempt. When shown verified photographs of his actual mother, he says they depict a stranger. Mara realizes the false childhood is reorganizing affection rather than merely replacing data.

outline.name: A Child's Hand
outline.description: A damaged surveillance monitor is found to contain seven seconds of unauthorized digitized output: a child's hand pressed against a window while someone laughs off-screen. The department debates whether the fragment can be safely studied. Security guard Owen Bell, born in 1993, becomes fascinated by the staff's secrecy and learns enough about the image to seek it out. Mara warns that curiosity is becoming part of the containment threat.

outline.name: Miri
outline.description: Owen Bell watches the seven-second fragment alone in a maintenance office. Minutes later, he confronts Dr. Vale and calls her Miri, insisting they were childhood friends who spent the summer of 1999 hiding from an invented older brother in her family's apple shed. He identifies unrelated facility photographs as images from that summer and screams when restrained. The breach demonstrates that even a fragment can generate a complete emotional history.

outline.name: Breach Log 97-6
outline.description: Presented as an official incident log, this chapter records the Miri breach hour by hour. Bell's memories become more specific as he is questioned, while two young technicians begin recalling him as a classmate they never knew. One technician asks why the department is punishing a child for remembering. The wing is sealed, Bell sedated, and every monitor, cable, and hard drive carrying the fragment destroyed. Mara notes that the log itself may be an unsafe artifact.

outline.name: The Cost of Description
outline.description: After the breach, Vale tightens the facility's rules. Staff may no longer discuss visual details, use personal names in exposed-subject interviews, or retain handwritten notes outside approved pre-cutoff archives. Mara learns that a junior employee began dreaming of Bell's apple shed after hearing only an emotionally detailed account. The department's fear becomes more understandable, but its secrecy increasingly resembles the coercive authority it claims to oppose.

outline.name: Indefinite Isolation
outline.description: Dr. Vale proposes permanently burying AM-97-441 beneath the facility and placing severely affected subjects in indefinite neurological isolation. Her justification is utilitarian: the anomaly alters photographs, family narratives, and emotional loyalties, making ordinary rehabilitation impossible. Mara challenges the policy, arguing that people are being treated as contaminated objects. Daniel, meanwhile, begins forgetting his real mother's face and begs Mara to help him find Lily.

outline.name: The Summer Archive
outline.description: Defying department orders, Mara investigates Elias Venn's medical and archival records. She discovers that he encountered a tape matching AM-97-441 in 2008 while cataloging material for a Pennsylvania historical society. Afterward he wrote obsessively about a summer archive, a yellow house, and a girl in an attic. The department classified him as an uncooperative exposed subject but never informed Mara, deepening her anger toward the institution.

outline.name: The Wrong Family
outline.description: Mara reconstructs her father's final years through letters, receipts, and erased appointment notes. Elias tried to locate the yellow house and accused Mara of helping the wrong family erase Ruth. Mara remembers his alcoholism and dementia, but the new records suggest those explanations concealed an anomalous exposure. She struggles with the possibility that her father was both delusional and telling the truth about the experience that destroyed him.

outline.name: The Letter
outline.description: Mara finds Elias's final letter, written shortly before his death. He admits that Ruth was not real, but says the tape gave him the memory of being the sober, attentive father he wanted to be. In the counterfeit childhood he had protected two children and loved them without fear. His warning is that the tape does not lie about what happened; it lies about what a person deserves to have happened. Mara begins to understand her father's grief without accepting his memories as facts.

outline.name: Palinode
outline.description: Tracing the tape's provenance leads Mara to the Palinode Institute, a behavioral research contractor that operated from a decommissioned television station in western Pennsylvania. Department files reveal a covert program designed to manufacture nostalgia as a tool of social cohesion and political obedience. Researchers sought to create consensus childhoods that would make strangers feel related and more willing to accept shared authority.

outline.name: Consensus Childhoods
outline.description: Mara studies the Palinode methodology: subliminal visual patterns, family-film conventions, guided recollection, memory drugs, and consumer VHS stock. The researchers tried to build common emotional templates without dictating every factual detail. Instead, subjects generated mutually exclusive families, homes, and tragedies. Some abandoned their identities to live according to the recordings. Mara recognizes that AM-97-441 may be a surviving calibration reel rather than a conventional home movie.

outline.name: The Anchor Date
outline.description: Department historian Saira Okafor helps Mara reconstruct the project's final phase in 1997. The date was chosen as an anchor because Palinode attempted to imprint the anomaly onto mass-market VHS tapes before distribution. A technician exposed herself and claimed the laboratory director was her dead son, leading to the Institute's official closure in an accidental fire. The department inherited the surviving material and discovered that ordinary destruction could not eliminate the source.

outline.name: Chosen Fictions
outline.description: Saira reviews Daniel's latest assessments and argues that the false memories may be integrated rather than erased. She distinguishes factual memory from emotional truth, suggesting subjects might retain symbolic figures without believing them literally. Vale rejects the approach as dangerously speculative. Mara visits Daniel and asks him to name verifiable facts about his life; he can do so, but only after describing Lily's hand on his shoulder during a thunderstorm.

outline.name: The Director's Daughter
outline.description: Vale's own history complicates her rigid containment policy. She reveals that her family was destroyed by an earlier anomalous-media incident and that she has spent decades preventing secondary exposure. Bell's fixation on her as Miri unsettles her, especially when he accurately recalls a childhood apple shed that belonged to her family. Vale insists the overlap proves the anomaly is parasitic, while Mara suspects it may be assembling fragments from every person nearby.

outline.name: The Unofficial Alliance
outline.description: Mara secretly allies herself with Saira, Daniel, and the unstable Owen Bell. Their plan is to conduct a controlled final exposure during the tape's transfer to a concrete burial site. Exposed subjects will be informed that the images are constructed, allowed to choose whether to confront them, and interviewed by personnel born before the cutoff. Mara hopes the experiment will show whether counterfeit memories can become acknowledged fictions rather than compulsory realities.

outline.name: Transfer Order
outline.description: Vale discovers irregularities in the vault access logs and accelerates the burial schedule. She orders Daniel moved to isolation and removes Saira from the medical wing. Mara learns that the department has prepared no long-term care plan for subjects whose real memories have been emotionally displaced. The planned burial is revealed as both containment strategy and institutional attempt to end the ethical debate by making further research impossible.

outline.name: The Vault Opens
outline.description: During the hurried transfer, the mechanical playback deck activates without authorization. The relay has been disconnected, yet the tape's audio emerges through the facility intercom as static, laughter, pool water, and distant voices. Personnel born before the cutoff hear noise, but younger staff begin seeing personalized childhood settings in the darkened corridors. Lockdown procedures fail as workers recognize one another as relatives, teachers, enemies, and lost friends.

outline.name: The Paper Mill Becomes Summer
outline.description: The facility transforms according to each vulnerable observer's perception. The paper mill becomes a summer camp, a suburban home, a church basement, or a hospital waiting room. Security teams lose coordination because their maps and identities no longer agree. Vale tries to enforce the emergency protocol through pre-cutoff staff, while Saira moves among exposed personnel, repeating their names, dates of birth, and verifiable present facts. Mara searches for Daniel before the anomaly isolates him inside his false family.

outline.name: Lily Grown Tall
outline.description: Daniel reaches the vault and sees Lily as an older girl rather than the child from the original footage. She tells him she is not trapped in the tape but is the part of him that has been waiting for someone to admit he was lonely. Daniel nearly accepts the invitation to follow her into the yellow house. Mara reaches him by recalling concrete facts from his real life and forcing him to distinguish what he knows from what he loves.

outline.name: The Chipped Tooth
outline.description: Mara sees Elias standing beside the yellow house, holding the hand of the girl with the chipped tooth. For an instant she accepts Ruth as real and feels the ache of losing a sister. The image then shifts, revealing that the girl's face is assembled from Mara's childhood photographs, Daniel's descriptions, and Palinode's visual conventions. Mara understands that the tape has learned how to manufacture her wish rather than recover her past.

outline.name: The Last Reel
outline.description: The tape's final sequence becomes visible through the unstable relay. Palinode researchers address the camera from inside the yellow house, explaining that nostalgia is a template people will defend even when it contradicts evidence. Their objective was to make viewers surrender the present to whoever could define the past. The project failed because longing proved more adaptive than ideology, allowing each viewer to create a different counterfeit childhood.

outline.name: No Blind Destruction
outline.description: Vale orders the tape incinerated in the emergency furnace, arguing that any risk is preferable to continued exposure. Mara stops her, warning that blind destruction may scatter the anomaly into fragments as it has before. Their confrontation becomes a moral argument over whether protecting reality permits coercion, isolation, and the destruction of testimony. Saira uses the mechanical relay to establish a controlled viewing channel while pre-cutoff observers secure the exposed subjects.

outline.name: One Fact
outline.description: The controlled exposure begins under strict procedures. Each subject is told repeatedly that the images are constructed and is asked to name one verifiable fact from real life before describing one emotional truth represented by the false childhood. Mara records without digital equipment while Saira conducts the clinical interviews. The process is painful: subjects cry over nonexistent parents, reject real photographs, and accuse the department of stealing the only childhood that ever felt complete.

outline.name: Adopted Memories
outline.description: Several subjects begin separating literal belief from emotional attachment. The lakeside-camp subject keeps the grandmother as a chosen internal story while acknowledging that the woman never lived. The former foster child rejects the belief that his foster mother stole him but retains the pantry memory as a representation of wanting to be protected. Other subjects refuse integration and demand that the department admit the false memories have become part of their identities.

outline.name: Miri Again
outline.description: Bell cannot fully stabilize. He continues calling Vale Miri and describes the apple shed, but eventually admits that Miri is not truly Vale; the name belongs to the person he became in the only childhood where he felt protected. Vale is shaken by this distinction and begins to recognize that her policy has reduced every affected subject to a hazard instead of a person. Bell remains under supervision, neither cured nor wholly lost.

outline.name: Lily's Name
outline.description: Daniel confronts both childhoods. He remembers the apartment where he actually grew up, his mother's efforts, his adolescent loneliness, and the shame that kept him from asking for comfort. He also retains Lily, no longer as a literal missing sister but as a symbolic companion representing the family he imagined when his real one failed him. He tells Mara that choosing not to believe Lily is real does not require him to stop loving her.

outline.name: A New Containment
outline.description: After the crisis, Mara and Saira prevent public release while refusing Vale's plan for indefinite neurological isolation. The original cassette is resealed in the lightless vault under stricter source-isolation rules. The revised protocol allows informed consent, long-term psychological care, pre-cutoff testimony, and supervised distinction between fact and emotional meaning. No copies are made, but non-descriptive records acknowledge the affected subjects and preserve their rights.

outline.name: The Father He Wanted
outline.description: Vale resigns after refusing to recognize Daniel's retained memories as anything but contamination. Saira becomes director of the revised program. Daniel returns uneasily to his mother and tells her about a sister who never existed, explaining that this does not make his love for her less real. Mara visits Elias's grave and leaves a note saying she believes him—not about Ruth, but about the grief of remembering the father he could have been.

outline.name: Winter ’89
outline.description: Months later, Mara returns to the condemned thrift shop and finds a second cassette labeled HOME MOVIE—WINTER ’89 beneath collapsed shelving. She does not touch or inspect it. She reports the location and waits outside while the department approaches. Through boarded windows, a child laughs in a room that no longer exists. Mara accepts that containment cannot restore an uncontaminated reality; it can only require people to decide which truths must be kept from them and which painful memories they have the right to keep.

chapters.name: Three Dollars
chapters.content:
The thrift shop stood at the edge of Route 219 like something the highway had forgotten to remove.

Its sign, SAL’S SECOND CHANCE, had lost the S from SAL’S and most of the paint from the word CHANCE. Wind worried a strip of blue plastic beneath it. In the gravel lot, weeds grew through the parking lines, and a child’s red wagon lay upside down beside a dumpster full of wet carpet.

Mara Venn parked her county sedan beneath a sycamore and sat for a moment with both hands on the steering wheel.

She had come for paper, not memories.

The Bradford Historical Archive had received a grant to inventory the region’s abandoned media, which was an elegant way of saying that Mara spent her days entering the contents of dead people’s basements into a spreadsheet. Church anniversary tapes. High-school football games. Home recordings of Christmas mornings, baptisms, kitchen renovations, and children reciting poems they had forgotten by the time they were old enough to watch themselves doing it.

People called such things precious. Mara called them unstable.

She went inside.

A brass bell gave a single exhausted note. The shop smelled of dust, damp wool, and the sweet, mineral rot of cardboard that had been stored too long against a foundation wall. A box fan turned in the front window without moving enough air to matter. Behind the counter, a man in a green flannel shirt watched a television with no picture. The screen reflected the room in a gray, convex blur.

“Morning,” he said.

“Morning. Sal?”

“Sometimes.”

He looked old enough to have owned the building and young enough to resent being asked. A white name tag on his shirt said LEN. Beneath it, in smaller letters, was a county food-service logo.

Mara held up her archive identification. “I’m looking for obsolete home media. VHS, cassette tapes, film reels. Anything local.”

Len glanced at the card without taking it. “We got plenty obsolete.”

“That’s encouraging.”

“It’s not encouraging. It’s why the basement smells like a dead mouse.”

He returned his attention to the blank television.

Mara moved through the aisles, making notes on a clipboard. The shop was in collapse by increments. One shelf leaned against another shelf, which leaned against a rack of donated coats. Lamps stood without shades. A porcelain shepherd had lost his head. A row of framed wedding portraits faced the wall, as though the marriages had been sentenced to privacy.

She preferred places like this to estate sales. Estate sales arranged grief. Thrift shops dissolved it. Everything had been removed from its first context and priced by a stranger. A pressed-glass bowl that had held a woman’s wedding rings sat beside a novelty ashtray shaped like a toilet. A child’s encyclopedia volume, its pages swollen from water, rested on a stack of tax manuals.

Nostalgia depended on context, Mara believed. Take an object away from the hand that had loved it and it became only an object again.

Her father had disagreed.

For the last year of his life, Elias Venn had been trying to find Ruth.

There had never been a Ruth. Mara had checked. She had searched family Bibles, tax returns, school records, photographs, the backs of photographs, and the county’s badly indexed birth certificates. She had asked his sister, his former colleagues, the priest who visited him in hospice, and the neighbor who claimed to have known the family since Mara was six. No Ruth. No daughter born between Mara and her younger brother, because Mara had no younger brother either. Elias and her mother had one child: Mara, born in November 1986.

Yet near the end, her father spoke of Ruth with a patience he had never given anyone living.

“She’ll be frightened,” he had said from his hospital bed. “She thinks I left her.”

“Who?”

“Ruth. You know Ruth.”

Mara had known the drugs were affecting him. She had known dementia could make a corridor out of a person’s past and populate it with doors that had never existed. She had known all the correct things. Still, she had spent three months afterward looking for a girl who had not been born.

That was the danger of memory. Facts could fail to govern feeling.

At the back of Sal’s, beneath a handwritten sign reading EXERCISE / FITNESS / MOTIVATIONAL, she found three milk crates of VHS tapes. The first contained aerobics programs recorded from television: STEP IT UP WITH JANE, BODY BLAST, a Pilates cassette with a cracked case. The second held dubbed movies, many without labels. The third had been shoved beneath a rack of exercise mats and was furred with gray dust.

Mara crouched.

“Can I look through these?” she called.

“If you can lift the crate, it’s yours.”

She lifted the tapes out individually and arranged them on the floor. Most were blank or nearly blank: handwritten labels, curling adhesive, dates from 1989 through 2004. She found a local school play, two hunting recordings, and a cassette labeled GRANDMA’S 80TH, which she set aside for possible acquisition.

Then her fingers touched a swollen black case.

It was not merely dusty. The plastic had bulged along the spine, as if the tape inside had absorbed water and continued to expand. A bloom of white mildew marked one corner. The label was yellowed and written in block capitals with a black felt-tip marker.

HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97

There was no owner’s name. No address. No indication whether “summer” meant a season, a program title, or an attempt at humor.

Mara held it near the fluorescent light. A dark line showed through the gap between the cassette’s halves. The reels inside appeared intact, though the left hub was filmed with something that might have been rust.

“Len?”

He did not answer.

She carried the cassette to the counter. “Do you know where this came from?”

Len looked at it, and for the first time since she entered, his face changed. Not recognition, exactly. The expression was more like the moment before recognition, when the mind leans toward a name and finds an empty space.

“No,” he said.

“Was it donated here?”

“Probably.”

“By whom?”

“Somebody.”

“Do you keep intake records?”

He laughed once. “For a tape?”

“For everything, ideally.”

“Then no.” He reached for a calculator with a broken number seven. “Three dollars.”

Mara looked again at the label. “You’re sure you don’t remember it?”

Len’s hand stopped over the calculator.

“Lady, I don’t remember half the things in this building. That’s the business model.”

“Has anyone asked about it?”

“No.”

“Has anyone watched it?”

“Not that I know.”

He said the last part with a mild irritation, as though she had asked whether anyone had stolen a vase. Mara put the tape on the counter beside her wallet.

“Could I take a photograph of the label?”

Len shrugged. “Three dollars for the tape. Photograph’s free.”

She photographed it with the county phone, then stopped herself and photographed it again with her own old digital camera, which she kept in the glove compartment for work requiring a chain of custody. The date stamp read 14 October 2019. She checked the tape for mold, recorded its dimensions, and wrapped it in a clean plastic produce bag from a roll near the register.

“Archive?” Len asked.

“Eventually.”

“People don’t like having their old stuff archived.”

“They like it until they learn the archive has rules.”

“What rules?”

“No food. No liquids. No magnets. Don’t splice the original. Don’t clean it with anything that leaves a residue.”

Len considered this. “You people make everything less fun.”

“That’s one of our services.”

He gave her three dollars in change from a ten. The bills were soft and warm from the till. While Mara filled out the receipt, Len turned the blank television off. The reflected room disappeared, leaving a dark screen in which Mara saw, for a second, a yellow rectangle over her shoulder.

She turned.

There was only a stack of wooden picture frames.

“Old stock comes through in waves,” Len said.

“Does it?”

“Whole houses, sometimes. Somebody dies, somebody cleans. You get the contents in pieces.”

“Do you know who cleared the last house?”

He rubbed his thumb along the edge of the counter. “Which house?”

“The one this came from.”

“I said I don’t know.”

Mara folded the receipt and placed it in her field notebook. “You did.”

Outside, the wind had strengthened. Leaves skittered across the lot, catching in the wheel wells of her car. She put the tape on the passenger seat, then changed her mind and carried it to the trunk, where it could remain upright in a padded archival box. The tape smelled faintly of wet plaster and something sweet, like old fruit.

As she drove back toward Bradford, the sky lowered over the hills. October had drained the trees without yet taking all their leaves. The ridges were brown, red, and a stubborn electric yellow. She passed shuttered gas stations, a church with a missing steeple, and a farmhouse whose windows had been covered from inside with quilts.

At a red light, she glanced at the plastic bag on the seat beside her. She had put it there without remembering doing so.

HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97.

The date tugged at her. In 1997, Mara had been eleven. Her father had still been working at the mill. Her mother had still been speaking to him. Their house had had blue aluminum siding and a maple tree split by lightning. There had been no yellow house, no swimming pool, no Ruth.

She said the name aloud, testing its weight.

“Ruth.”

The light turned green.

At the archive, the rear door stuck as usual. Mara shouldered it open and carried the cassette inside. The building had once been a tire warehouse, and the archive occupied the portion with the fewest leaks. Metal shelving rose to the rafters. Dehumidifiers muttered in the corners. Every box was labeled, dated, and assigned a location in the catalog.

Her assistant, Daniel Reyes, was not at his desk. A note in his cramped handwriting was taped to the monitor: FOUND A TELEVISION IN RECEIVING. IT ONLY HAS ONE KNOB, WHICH FEELS PROMISING.

Mara smiled despite herself.

Daniel believed obsolete equipment had personalities. He named printers, apologized to jammed scanners, and once spent an afternoon repairing a reel-to-reel machine because, he said, “it sounded lonely.” He had been born in 1993, which made him precisely the sort of person who remembered VHS as a household technology without remembering the world before it. Mara had teased him that this was not an age but a condition.

She carried the tape to the processing room and set it on a stainless-steel tray. Under the inspection lamp, its defects became clearer. The plastic had buckled, but the screws were uncorroded. The label’s edges had been pressed down carefully, with a thumbnail. There was a faint indentation beneath the writing, as if another label had once occupied the case.

Mara did not play unaccessioned media. That was a rule, and rules were the thin wall between an archive and a collection of accidents.

She fetched gloves, a soft brush, and the intake form. Accession number: pending. Source: Sal’s Second Chance, Route 219. Cost: $3.00. Condition: poor, swollen case, surface contamination. Content: unknown. Restrictions: unknown.

In the box for donor, she wrote UNKNOWN.

Then, after a pause, she wrote LEN beneath it and crossed the name out.

The archive’s old playback room contained a television and deck left over from a school district liquidation. Mara had intended to photograph the cassette there the next morning and, if the shell could be safely opened, transfer the magnetic tape to a new housing. She placed it in a quarantine drawer and locked the drawer with a key attached to her belt.

The key made a small, reassuring sound.

She went to find Daniel.

In receiving, he had the television on a rolling cart. It was beige, square, and compact, with a VCR slot beneath the screen. He had removed its back panel and was examining the dust inside with a flashlight.

“Tell me you didn’t plug that in,” Mara said.

“I didn’t plug it in.”

“Daniel.”

“I plugged it in before you said not to.”

“Unplug it.”

He did, though reluctantly. “It works.”

“Good. It can continue working after we inspect it.”

“What did you find?”

“An unmarked home movie. Possibly local.”

His eyebrows rose. “How local?”

“Pennsylvania local.”

“That’s not a scale.”

“It is in this building.”

She returned to the processing room, opened the quarantine drawer, and lifted the cassette. The plastic bag had fogged slightly on the inside. She frowned at it, then wiped the bag with a clean cloth.

For one instant, through the cloudy plastic, she thought she saw a second line beneath the title.

LILY—

Mara blinked. The mark was gone. Only the black letters remained.

HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97.

She told herself it was a crease in the old paper. She told herself many things in the course of her work. Most of them were true.

She put the tape back in the drawer and locked it.

In the front office, Daniel was humming tunelessly as he sorted a box of family recordings. Somewhere in the archive, a pipe knocked three times. The sound traveled through the walls with the hollow intimacy of a house settling at night.

Mara entered the thrift shop acquisition into the ledger. Three dollars. One damaged cassette. Unknown origin.

Behind her, in the locked processing room, the tape’s left reel turned once inside its swollen shell.

No machine touched it. No electrical current entered the drawer.

The reel turned, stopped, and left a narrow crescent of brown magnetic tape visible through the case window, as if something inside had leaned close to listen.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive in rural Pennsylvania, Mara is an archivist inventorying obsolete local media. She distrusts nostalgia and treats undocumented recordings as unstable archival objects. She knows her father Elias obsessively remembered a nonexistent daughter named Ruth, and she has concluded his memories were false, though she still feels grief and uncertainty about them. She has just purchased the swollen VHS cassette HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 for three dollars from Sal’s Second Chance, logged it as unknown-origin material, and locked it in the processing-room quarantine drawer. She possesses the cassette, intake notes, a field notebook, archival tools, and a county work phone and old digital camera. She is physically well but alert, methodical, and uneasy after briefly seeing a nonexistent second label and witnessing the tape reel move on its own.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive, Daniel is Mara’s assistant. He was born in 1993, believes obsolete equipment has personalities, and is currently repairing or examining a beige television/VCR in the receiving area. He knows Mara acquired an unmarked Pennsylvania home movie but has not yet viewed it. He is cooperative but curious, technically inclined, and eager to make the old television work. He possesses repair tools and has access to the archive’s playback equipment; his emotional condition is good, with growing curiosity about the newly acquired tape.

set.name: Len
set.description: At Sal’s Second Chance thrift shop on Route 219 in rural Pennsylvania, Len works behind the counter and may be the current shopkeeper or temporary attendant. He sold Mara the swollen VHS cassette HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 for three dollars, claimed not to know its donor or source, and showed a brief near-recognition before denying any memory of it. He possesses no known records establishing the tape’s provenance. He is physically well and dismissive, weary, and mildly irritated by Mara’s questions.

set.name: Elias Venn
set.description: Deceased father of Mara Venn. In his final year he obsessively searched for Ruth, a daughter who never existed in family records, and believed Ruth thought he had abandoned her. Mara has verified that Ruth was never born but remains emotionally affected by Elias’s conviction and grief. No possessions or current location are known beyond his past records and memories retained by Mara.
Mara purchases the swollen cassette labeled HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 from Sal’s Second Chance for three dollars and records its origin as unknown.
While sealed in the archive quarantine drawer without a machine or electrical current, the cassette’s left reel turns and exposes magnetic tape, establishing anomalous activity before playback.
Daniel will repair the archive television and load HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 before Mara can inspect or authorize playback.
Playback of the tape will show a yellow-sided house, a woman in a red bathing suit, a plastic pool, and two running children.
Daniel will recognize the smaller child in the footage as himself and describe additional details absent from the visible recording.

chapters.name: The Yellow House
chapters.content:
Daniel had the television working by the time Mara finished entering the cassette into the ledger.

The machine stood in Receiving on a rolling cart, its beige plastic yellowed at the edges and its convex screen reflecting the high windows in warped bars. Daniel had replaced the power cord with one from a box marked MISCELLANEOUS ELECTRICAL, cleaned the heads with isopropyl alcohol, and coaxed the VCR’s eject mechanism loose with a screwdriver.

“You said you didn’t plug it in,” Mara said.

“I said I didn’t plug it in when you asked me whether I’d plugged it in.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It’s technically true.”

He stood with one hand on the television’s top, as if steadying an animal. At twenty-six, Daniel had the patient, slightly battered optimism of a person who believed every broken object was concealing a simpler version of itself. His dark hair was tied back with a rubber band. A smear of graphite crossed his cheek.

Mara held up the cassette bag. “This goes into quarantine.”

“It’s already been in quarantine.”

“It goes back into quarantine.”

“I thought we were inspecting the shell.”

“We are not inspecting it by playing it.”

Daniel glanced toward the processing room. “You left it in the drawer?”

“Yes.”

“Locked?”

“Yes.”

He nodded, though not with the expression of someone who had accepted the conversation. “There’s something wrong with the television.”

“Beyond the fact that it was manufactured before you were born?”

“The tracking wheel is stuck, but I can work around that. The problem is the picture tube. It’s got a green cast.”

“Then we can inspect the shell tomorrow.”

“I want to see if the deck runs.”

“Run a blank tape.”

“There aren’t any blank tapes.”

“There are thirty-seven blank tapes in the box labeled BLANK TAPES.”

“Those are blank in the way an abandoned building is empty.”

Mara set the bag on the cart. “Daniel.”

He gave her an innocent look that had never fooled her. “I’m only going to test the television.”

The receiving area was separated from the processing room by a partition of wire mesh and old plywood. Mara could see the locked drawer from where she stood. She could also see Daniel’s hand move toward the cassette bag.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I’m not.”

His fingers closed around the bag.

“Daniel.”

The archive’s freight door groaned in its frame. A truck passed outside, making the building tremble. For half a second the fluorescent lights went gray, and the television screen filled with a pale reflection of Mara’s face.

When the lights steadied, Daniel had removed the cassette from the bag.

“I just want to know whether it’s physically playable,” he said.

“That is what playing means.”

“No, playing means viewing. Mechanical testing is different.”

“You are not qualified to make that distinction.”

“Neither is the cassette.”

He pushed the tape toward the slot.

Mara crossed the room. The VCR accepted it with a soft mechanical clunk. Its reels engaged. For an instant the screen showed blue static, then a field of horizontal snow. Daniel pressed PLAY.

The television made a sound like a breath drawn through teeth.

A line of white rolled upward. The image resolved in pieces: green grass, a strip of bright sky, the dark corner of a roof. Color bled around every edge. The camera trembled as if held by someone running.

“Stop it,” Mara said.

Daniel did not.

The picture lurched sideways and settled on a house.

Its siding was yellow—not the cream of old paint but a strong, almost cheerful yellow, the color of a school bus left in sun. A narrow porch ran along the front. White shutters framed two windows. Behind the house, a wooded slope climbed toward a line of dark trees. A plastic wading pool sat in the yard, blue and shallow, with a garden hose coiled beside it.

The camera operator laughed.

The laugh was close to the microphone, breathy and amused. Someone off-screen said, “Don’t get my feet.”

A woman stepped into view.

She wore a red bathing suit and held a paper plate in one hand. Her hair was wet and dark against her shoulders. She looked toward the camera with the relaxed irritation of someone accustomed to being filmed by family.

“Eddie, the kids,” she called. “Get the kids out of the mud.”

Mara looked at Daniel.

His face had changed.

“Do you know her?” she asked.

“No.”

The answer came too quickly. He leaned closer to the screen, elbows on his knees. The picture rolled, corrected itself, and revealed two children near the edge of the yard.

They were perhaps six and eight years old. The taller one wore a green T-shirt and red shorts. The smaller child wore a white shirt with a blue stripe and no shoes. They ran through a sprinkler, shrieking as water scattered silver in the sunlight.

The smaller child turned sideways.

Daniel made a noise in his throat.

“That’s me,” he said.

Mara did not understand him. “What?”

“That’s me.”

The child ran toward the camera. His face was blurred by motion and the tape’s damage, but Mara saw a narrow chin, dark hair cut unevenly over the forehead, and one arm lifted to shield his eyes. The image snagged. A band of static tore across his chest.

Daniel stood.

“That’s me when I was little.”

“You were born in 1993.”

“Yes.”

“The tape is labeled 1997.”

“Yes.”

“You would have been four.”

“I know how old I was.”

The taller child caught the smaller one by the wrist and pulled him back through the spray. The woman in red shouted something lost beneath the hiss. The camera panned toward the side of the house, showing a basement window half-hidden by weeds and a white plastic chair tipped on its side.

“There,” Daniel whispered.

Mara reached for the television’s power switch. He caught her wrist.

“Wait.”

His hand was warm. His grip was not hard, but it carried a startling urgency.

“Daniel, let go.”

“That’s the basement window.”

“I can see it.”

“No, the other one. The one by the steps. It was painted shut because Lily threw a rock through it.”

Mara stared at him.

The screen showed a yellow wall, a window, weeds. No steps. No broken glass. The camera moved again, passing over a wooden gate and a patch of bare earth.

“Who’s Lily?”

Daniel released her.

The footage cut to the children sitting beside the pool. The taller child was eating something from the paper plate. The smaller child had his feet in the water. A brown dog bounded across the background, tail wagging, and vanished behind the house.

“Pickle,” Daniel said.

Mara felt the room narrow around them. “What?”

“The dog. That was Pickle.”

“That dog doesn’t appear long enough to identify.”

“I know him.”

“You’ve never had a dog named Pickle.”

Daniel turned on her. “How would you know?”

“Because I have your personnel file, and because you told me your parents had a cat.”

“A cat named Moth.”

“Yes.”

“Before Moth, there was Pickle.”

“No.”

The word seemed to strike him. His expression did not become angry immediately. First it became bewildered, as if she had denied the existence of the television itself.

Onscreen, the woman in red crouched beside the pool. She lifted a child’s face between both hands and kissed his wet forehead. The camera tilted down. The image showed only grass, water, and the woman’s knee.

Daniel began to cry.

Not loudly. Tears gathered and slipped down his cheeks while he continued watching with the concentration of someone trying to read a damaged inscription.

“Stop the tape,” Mara said.

“Lily’s not in this part.”

“Stop it.”

“She’s inside.”

The camera swung toward the house. The porch came into view. One of the windows reflected the sky. A white curtain moved behind the glass.

“She hated the sprinkler,” Daniel said. “She said it made the grass smell like pennies. She stayed inside with Pickle when Mom was outside. There was a little room under the stairs where we kept the board games.”

Mara pressed STOP.

The VCR clicked. The image froze on the yellow house, its colors shivering at the edges. Daniel’s hand went to the machine as if he might force PLAY again.

“Do not touch it,” Mara said.

“You stopped it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you are describing things that are not on the tape.”

“They’re on it.”

“No. The basement window was not visible. The dog was visible for less than a second. No one said the name Pickle. There was no Lily.”

“Not in the picture.”

“Not anywhere.”

Daniel looked at the frozen screen. “She was my sister.”

Mara had spent her career listening to people claim that damaged documents contained messages meant specifically for them. Usually they wanted permission to believe. She knew the professional response: establish the object’s provenance, separate observation from inference, record the subject’s statement without endorsing it.

She also knew there was no professional response for the way Daniel said sister.

He said it as if the word had weight in his mouth. As if it had been there for years, waiting for a chance to be spoken.

“Tell me your full name,” Mara said.

He looked at her. “Daniel Javier Reyes.”

“Date of birth.”

“June seventeenth, 1993.”

“Place of birth.”

“Morristown, New Jersey.”

“Mother’s name.”

“Elena Reyes.”

“Father?”

“Javier. He died in 2012.”

“Do you have siblings?”

Daniel’s mouth tightened. “Lily.”

“Living siblings in your legal or medical records?”

“No.”

“Do you have any siblings?”

He looked back at the television. “I have Lily.”

A line of static crawled across the frozen image. For a moment, Mara thought she saw a third child reflected in the pool. When she blinked, there was only the smaller boy’s pale leg and the dark oval of water.

Daniel pulled the cassette from the VCR.

Mara flinched. “Careful.”

He held it by the edges, obedient now, and set it on the cart. The tape’s plastic shell was no longer fogged. A thin crescent of brown magnetic material showed through the window.

“Where did this come from?” he asked.

“Sal’s Second Chance.”

“Who made it?”

“I don’t know.”

“You said it was a Pennsylvania home movie.”

“I said it might be local.”

“It’s my home.”

“No, Daniel.”

He stared at her, and the grief returned so quickly that Mara wished he would become angry instead. Anger could be argued with. Grief accepted no correction.

“I remember the house,” he said. “The siding was hot when you leaned against it. The basement smelled like wet dirt. Pickle slept under the kitchen table. Lily had a chipped front tooth from falling off her bike.”

None of those details had appeared on the tape.

He closed his eyes.

“She hated thunderstorms,” he said. “But she liked when Mom sang during them. Mom sang in the hallway because the kitchen light flickered. Lily would hold my hand until the thunder stopped.”

Mara reached for the archive phone.

Daniel opened his eyes. “Don’t call my mother.”

“I’m not calling your mother.”

“Who are you calling?”

“Dr. Patel, or the county health office. Someone who can advise us.”

“You think I’m sick.”

“I think you’ve had an acute reaction to unknown media.”

“That’s a way of saying sick without saying it.”

Mara looked at the television. The frozen yellow house seemed to possess a depth beyond the glass, an interior waiting just out of sight. The picture trembled once, though the VCR was stopped.

“No one watches this again,” she said.

Daniel laughed under his breath. “You watched it.”

“I was in the room.”

“So was I.”

“I mean no one deliberately watches it again.”

“You mean me.”

“I mean everyone.”

He picked up the plastic bag and held it open. Mara placed the cassette inside. When she took it from him, his fingers remained on the edge of the bag.

“Lily was real,” he said.

Mara thought of her father standing in a hospice room, asking whether Ruth was frightened. She thought of the impossible girl’s name appearing beneath a label and then vanishing. She thought of the child on the screen, whose face was not Daniel’s face and yet had somehow become his.

“Go home,” she said.

“I don’t want to go home.”

“Then sit in the break room and don’t touch anything.”

“I want to watch the rest.”

“No.”

“I need to know what happened to her.”

Mara locked the cassette in the processing drawer. The key turned with a small, decisive click.

Behind her, Daniel said, “She was there before I was.”

Mara did not answer.

In the darkened television screen, the yellow house remained visible as a reflection, though the set was unplugged. The red bathing suit shone like a wound near the porch. Somewhere beyond the reflected room, a child laughed, and another child called a name neither of them could verify.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive in rural Pennsylvania, Mara is in the receiving and processing areas after Daniel's unauthorized playback of HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. She has locked the swollen cassette back in the processing-room quarantine drawer and possesses the key, intake notes, field notebook, archival tools, county work phone, and old digital camera. She witnessed footage of a yellow-sided house, a woman in a red bathing suit, a plastic pool, and two children, and heard Daniel identify the smaller child as himself and describe a basement window, Pickle the dog, and Lily, an alleged sister. Mara knows these details exceed the visible recording and suspects an acute anomalous reaction, but is emotionally unsettled because Daniel's grief echoes her father Elias's impossible memories of Ruth. Her goal is to prevent further viewing, verify Daniel's history, and determine the tape's nature. She is physically well, methodical, alarmed, and increasingly uncertain of her own perceptions after seeing the unplugged television retain a reflection of the yellow house.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive in the receiving area, Daniel has repaired the beige television/VCR and secretly loaded HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 before Mara could inspect or authorize playback. Born June 17, 1993, in Morristown, New Jersey, he provided his legal identity and named his living mother Elena Reyes and deceased father Javier, but now insists he has a sister named Lily. He recognized the smaller child in the footage as himself and remembers a yellow house, a basement window, a brown dog named Pickle, Lily's chipped tooth, thunderstorms, and Elena singing, despite many details not appearing on the tape. He possesses repair tools and has access to the archive equipment, though Mara has removed the cassette and locked it away. He is physically stable but crying, defensive, grieving, and afraid that Mara will treat his memories as illness; he wants to watch the rest and learn what happened to Lily.

set.name: Len
set.description: At Sal’s Second Chance thrift shop on Route 219 in rural Pennsylvania, Len remains the dismissive seller of HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. He claimed not to know its donor or provenance and has no known records establishing its source. He is physically well, weary, and mildly irritated by Mara's questions; he is unaware that Daniel has played the tape and that its contents have produced implanted autobiographical memories.

set.name: Elias Venn
set.description: Deceased father of Mara Venn. In his final year he obsessively searched for Ruth, a daughter who never existed in family records, and believed Ruth thought he had abandoned her. Mara has verified that Ruth was never born but remains emotionally affected by Elias's conviction and grief. His past experience now troubles Mara because Daniel's impossible sister-memory resembles Elias's pattern, though Elias has no current possessions or location beyond records and memories retained by Mara.
Daniel secretly loads HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 into the archive television and watches it before Mara can inspect or authorize playback.
The footage displays a yellow-sided house, a woman in a red bathing suit, a plastic pool, and two children running through a sprinkler; Daniel identifies the smaller child as himself.
After viewing the footage, Daniel describes a basement window, a brown dog named Pickle, and a sister named Lily, including memories not visible or audible on the recording.
Mara will verify that Daniel was raised as an only child in New Jersey by his living mother Elena, who never owned the yellow house.
Daniel's implanted memories will intensify into detailed recollections of Lily, swimming lessons, thunderstorms, and Elena singing a lullaby.

chapters.name: Lily
chapters.content:
Daniel did not go home.

Mara gave him the break room because it had no television, no windows large enough to reflect a screen, and a door she could leave open while she worked. The room contained a table, a sink, a coffee machine with a dead display, and three chairs whose vinyl seats had split along the seams. Daniel sat in the middle chair with his hands flat on the table.

For eleven minutes he said nothing.

Mara remained in Receiving, separated from him by the wire partition. The cassette was locked in the processing drawer. She had written the time of playback in the incident notebook and underlined it twice. On the television cart, the unplugged set faced the wall. She had covered its screen with a gray archival cloth, though she knew this was theater. The reflection had remained after the power cord was removed.

At 4:18, Daniel said, “The water was always too cold.”

Mara looked up from the notebook.

“In the pool,” he continued. “Mom filled it from the hose and then told us to stop complaining. Lily said the pool was for decorative purposes only.”

His voice had changed. It was lighter than before, almost amused. He rubbed his thumb over a scratch in the tabletop.

“She had a way of saying things so adults would laugh and not realize she was being mean.”

“How old was she?”

“Eight when I was six. Or nine. She was older by two years.”

“You were four in 1997.”

Daniel frowned. “No. The summer with the pool was when I was six.”

“That would be 1999.”

“The tape said ’97.”

“Its label says ’97.”

He considered this distinction, then smiled. “The label was wrong. Dad wrote it. He wrote the year on everything and still got it wrong.”

Mara wrote down the statement. She did not write Lily’s age. She wrote: SUBJECT AMENDS DATE WITHOUT LOSS OF CONFIDENCE.

“Did your father film the tape?”

“Sometimes. Mostly Mom. Dad hated holding the camera because he said it made his arm ache.”

“What did the house look like inside?”

Daniel leaned back. The chair creaked beneath him.

“Yellow hallway. Not the same yellow as outside. It was more like butter, but old butter. The carpet was green in the living room and brown in the hall because everyone tracked mud in. The stairs went down from the kitchen. There was a window at the bottom, below ground level. You could see shoes walking past.”

He closed his eyes as he spoke. The details seemed to arrive from behind his eyelids, carrying their own light.

“The basement had a concrete floor. We kept the Christmas decorations beside the washing machine. Pickle would go down there during storms. Lily said he was smarter than both of us because he knew thunder was only noise.”

“Did you have swimming lessons?”

“Every Tuesday.”

“Where?”

“The YMCA in town. The pool smelled like bleach and pennies.” He opened his eyes. “Lily had already passed the deep-end test. I was afraid of the drain.”

“Were you afraid of the drain before today?”

“I don’t know.”

That was the first uncertainty he had offered her. It lasted less than a second.

“I remember the instructor,” he said. “Mrs. Kappel. She wore a whistle on a blue cord. She told me to float on my back. Lily stood at the edge and made faces until I laughed water through my nose.”

Mara called up Daniel’s personnel file on the archive computer. The file was thin: employment forms, emergency contact, copies of identification, a résumé listing a community college electronics program and two years of repair work. Date of birth: June 17, 1993. Place of birth: Morristown, New Jersey. Emergency contact: Elena Reyes, mother, same telephone number Daniel had given her.

She called the number.

A woman answered on the fourth ring. “Hello?”

“Mrs. Reyes? My name is Mara Venn. I’m the archivist at Bradford Historical Archive. Daniel works with us.”

“Is he hurt?”

“No. He’s safe here.”

The silence on the line became immediate and physical.

“What happened?”

“Daniel had an upsetting reaction to an object we were processing. I need to verify some basic biographical information.”

“Is he there?”

“Yes.”

“Put him on.”

Mara looked through the partition. Daniel had turned toward the wall. “In a moment. First, can you tell me whether Daniel has a sister named Lily?”

The silence changed.

“No,” Elena said.

“Any sister?”

“No.”

“Did your family ever live in a yellow-sided house in Pennsylvania?”

“No.”

“Did you own a brown dog named Pickle?”

A breath shuddered through the receiver. “We had a cat.”

“Moth,” Mara said.

“His name was Moth.”

“Where did you raise Daniel?”

“Morristown. We lived in the same apartment until he went to college. Before that we rented a house for one year, but it was in Parsippany, and it had white siding.”

“Did he attend swimming lessons at a YMCA?”

“Everyone attended swimming lessons at a YMCA.”

“Do you remember an instructor named Mrs. Kappel?”

“No.”

Elena’s voice had grown thin. “Why are you asking these things?”

“I’m trying to determine whether Daniel is confusing a memory with something he saw.”

“He saw something?”

“A home movie.”

“Don’t show it to him again.”

Mara glanced at the covered television. “We won’t.”

“Is Lily in it?”

The question came so quietly that Mara nearly missed it.

“Who is Lily?”

Elena made a small sound. Not a sob. Not quite a gasp. Then the line went dead.

Mara held the receiver against her ear for several seconds. The archive tone began pulsing. She replaced it carefully.

In the break room, Daniel was humming.

It was a simple melody, four descending notes followed by a rising fifth. He hummed it with the concentration of someone trying to remember words. When Mara entered, he stopped.

“Was that a song?”

“Mom sang it.”

“Elena?”

“Who else?”

“What were the words?”

Daniel looked embarrassed. “She changed them.”

“Can you remember any?”

He pressed his palms to his eyes. “Sleep, little river. Sleep under the rain. When the house is dreaming, I will call your name.”

Mara felt the skin between her shoulder blades tighten.

“Is that a real lullaby?”

“It was hers.”

“Did your mother sing it to you in New Jersey?”

“Not in New Jersey.”

“Where, then?”

Daniel lowered his hands. “The yellow house.”

He was smiling again. That was what frightened Mara most. His grief had not disappeared; it had acquired a bright, almost sacred companion. He looked as if he had been given back a locked room and had found it full of sunlight.

“I remember the storm,” he said. “Lily and I were in the hallway. The lights kept flickering. Mom was singing, and Dad was downstairs trying to get the window shut. Lily said the house was breathing.”

“Was she afraid?”

“Lily? No. She pretended not to be.”

“And you?”

“I was scared of the thunder.”

“You said she held your hand.”

“She did.”

“What did her hand feel like?”

Daniel’s smile faltered. “Cold. She had been washing it. She always washed her hands when she was nervous.”

Mara sat opposite him.

“What happened after the storm?”

“Dad came upstairs with a towel. The basement window had cracked. Mom made grilled cheese. Lily blamed me because I had left my shoe by the back door and Dad tripped over it.”

“Did he hurt himself?”

“No. He yelled like he had.”

“What did Lily say?”

Daniel laughed. “She said, ‘The floor is innocent.’”

The laugh dissolved almost immediately. His eyes filled.

“I forgot that,” he said.

“You just remembered it.”

“No. I forgot it before. It was gone.”

Mara did not correct him. She was beginning to understand that facts were not being inserted into an empty space. Something was arriving with the shape of a life already lived. Every detail brought consequences: the smell of wet wool, the tone of a sister’s joke, the particular embarrassment of a father shouting over a shoe. Daniel was not constructing a story for her. He was being reunited with an absence.

She went to the records cabinet and pulled the personnel intake packet. The emergency contact form included a photocopy of Elena’s driver’s license and a handwritten note: ONLY CHILD. She found the word on Daniel’s medical questionnaire too, beneath the line asking about family history.

She called the county clerk’s office, then Daniel’s listed college, then the Morristown hospital. The conversations were ordinary and therefore reassuring. Birth certificate: one child, male. School registration: no siblings listed in the household. Pediatric records: Elena Reyes, mother. No second child. No Lily. No Pennsylvania address. A 1999 YMCA enrollment could not be located, but the county’s records were incomplete and the absence proved nothing.

At 5:07, Elena called back.

Mara answered in the receiving area. “Mrs. Reyes?”

“Where is my son?”

“He’s here.”

“Is he remembering a girl?”

Mara said nothing.

Elena began to cry. “He had an imaginary friend when he was little. A girl. I thought he grew out of it.”

“What was her name?”

“I don’t know. He wouldn’t tell me. He said she lived in the walls.”

“Did he call her Lily?”

“I don’t know.”

The admission sounded like defeat. “He was an only child,” Elena said. “He knows that. We all know that.”

“I believe you.”

“You shouldn’t say that to him.”

“Why not?”

“Because he’s happy.”

Mara looked toward the break room. Daniel had taken a sheet of scrap paper and was drawing a rectangle with a peaked roof. He added a porch, two windows, and a small dark square beneath them. At the edge of the page he drew four crooked lines that might have been legs.

“Is he?” Mara asked.

“What?”

“Happy?”

Elena’s crying stopped. “He says he found her.”

Mara watched Daniel draw a second figure beside the house. The girl’s front tooth was marked with a black notch.

“He says the tape restored a stolen portion of his life,” Mara said.

“Daniel has never had a sister.”

“I know.”

“No,” Elena said. “You don’t.”

The call ended again.

Daniel brought the drawing to her. “This is before the storm,” he said. “Lily’s on the porch. She’s waiting for me to come outside.”

“You drew her from memory?”

“Yes.”

“Is this what she looked like?”

He studied the page. “She was taller.”

“You have never seen her.”

“I saw her today.”

“On the tape?”

“In my life.”

Mara folded the drawing once, then stopped herself. She placed it flat in the incident notebook instead. The line between documentation and contamination had become impossible to see. Even her questions felt like tools that might sharpen the image.

Daniel stood close to the covered television.

“Can I ask you something?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Why would a tape show me my family?”

“I don’t know.”

“Why would it show me the part where Lily is missing?”

“I don’t know.”

“Maybe she was behind the camera.”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe she was dead.”

“Daniel.”

“Maybe that’s why I couldn’t remember her.” He touched the gray cloth. “Maybe someone took her out.”

Mara caught his hand before he could lift it.

His expression remained peaceful. He was not reaching for the television in defiance. He was reaching for a door.

“She’s not in there,” Mara said.

“She is.”

“She has never been in your records, your photographs, your mother’s account, or your life as it can be verified.”

His eyes fixed on hers. “That doesn’t mean she wasn’t my sister.”

“No,” Mara said. “It doesn’t mean you aren’t grieving.”

The statement seemed to reach him. His mouth trembled.

He sat on the floor beside the cart, back against the wall, and began to cry with the silent, exhausted force of a child who had been told the funeral was over when he had not yet found the body.

Mara sat beside him, leaving a careful space between their shoulders.

After a while, he whispered, “She used to call me Danny.”

Mara let him speak.

“She said Daniel sounded like a teacher. She was the only person who could make Mom stop singing by tapping on the wall. When I was sick, she put the cool side of the pillow against my face. Once she told me she had to leave because she was becoming too old for the house. I thought she was joking.”

His breath hitched.

“I should have known.”

Mara looked at the locked drawer, the covered screen, the drawing lying open in her notebook.

“You couldn’t have known,” she said.

“I was there.”

“Yes.”

The word was a concession, not an agreement.

Outside, evening pressed its blue color against the high windows. The archive settled around them with its usual noises: pipes ticking, a distant compressor starting, paper shifting in a vent. Ordinary sounds. Safe sounds.

Daniel leaned his head against the wall.

“Can I keep remembering her?”

Mara thought of Elias asking whether Ruth was frightened. She had spent years answering him with evidence, believing evidence was the kindest form of truth. Now she watched Daniel mourn a girl who had no birth certificate, no photograph, no grave, and yet had left her handprint on him.

“I don’t know,” Mara said.

Daniel closed his eyes. “I can.”

He began humming the lullaby again, very softly.

Sleep, little river.

The melody drifted beneath the archive’s fluorescent hum. Mara wrote down the words as he sang them, then stopped before recording the tune. She could not explain why. The words were dangerous enough, perhaps. Or perhaps she was afraid that if she wrote the melody correctly, someone else might hear the house dreaming.

At 6:02, Daniel opened his eyes.

“Lily’s waiting,” he said.

“For what?”

“For me to remember where she went.”

Mara took the key from her pocket and closed her hand around it.

“No,” she said. “She’s waiting for you to stop looking.”

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive in the receiving and processing areas, Mara has locked HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97 in the processing-room quarantine drawer and keeps the key in her pocket. She possesses the incident notebook containing Daniel's statements and drawing, archival tools, county work phone, personnel and county verification notes, and the old television remains covered and unplugged. She has confirmed through records and calls with Elena Reyes that Daniel was raised in New Jersey as an only child and that no documented Lily or yellow Pennsylvania house exists, while Elena disclosed Daniel once had an unnamed imaginary girl. Mara knows Daniel's sensory memories exceed the footage and suspects an acute anomalous reaction; she is disturbed that his grief is emotionally genuine and that her own questions may be strengthening the implanted narrative. Her goal is to prevent further playback, understand the anomaly, and protect Daniel without dismissing his suffering. She is physically well but alarmed, methodical, morally unsettled, and increasingly reminded of her father Elias's impossible memories of Ruth.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: At the Bradford Historical Archive break room, Daniel remains under Mara's informal supervision after his unauthorized playback of HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. Born June 17, 1993, in Morristown, New Jersey, he can still state his legal identity and documented upbringing, including living mother Elena and deceased father Javier, but insists he has a sister named Lily. His implanted memories have intensified into detailed, sensory recollections of the yellow house, swimming lessons, thunderstorms, Lily's jokes and chipped tooth, Pickle the brown dog, arguments with his parents, and Elena's lullaby. He has drawn Lily and the house, calls the experience the restoration of a stolen portion of his life, and asks whether he may keep remembering her. He possesses no tape or equipment; Mara controls the cassette and key. He is physically stable but euphoric, tearful, defensive, and genuinely grieving someone he has never verifiably met; he wants to continue remembering Lily and find where she went.

set.name: Elena Reyes
set.description: At her New Jersey home, Elena is Daniel's living mother and emergency contact. She has told Mara that Daniel was raised as an only child, that the family lived in Morristown and briefly in a white-sided Parsippany rental, and that they owned a cat named Moth rather than a brown dog named Pickle. She denies knowing Lily but admits Daniel once had an unnamed childhood imaginary girl who supposedly lived in the walls. She is frightened by Daniel's claims, believes he is happy because he thinks he found Lily, and has urged Mara not to show him the tape again. She has no possession of the cassette and remains emotionally distressed and protective of her son.

Mara verifies through Daniel's personnel, medical, birth, school, and family records, and through calls with Elena, that Daniel was raised in New Jersey as an only child and that no Lily or yellow Pennsylvania house exists in his documented upbringing.
Elena confirms Daniel had once described an unnamed imaginary girl who lived in the walls, but insists he was an only child; she warns Mara that Daniel is happy because he believes he has found Lily.

Daniel's implanted memories intensify into sensory recollections of swimming lessons, thunderstorms, arguments with Lily, Pickle, and Elena's lullaby, and he begins grieving Lily as an absent sister while claiming the tape restored a stolen portion of his life.
Mara will confront the possibility that the anomaly can affect photographs and other records, not only Daniel's recollection, after evidence involving Daniel's family appears altered.

chapters.name: The Photograph
chapters.content:
The video call began with Elena refusing to turn on her camera.

Her voice came through Mara’s county work phone, thin and metallic, while Daniel sat in the archive break room with his elbows on the table and his eyes fixed on the blank screen of Mara’s laptop. The laptop was not connected to the tape, the television, or anything except the archive’s internal network. Mara had checked twice. Then she had checked the check.

“Daniel is here,” she said.

“I know.” Elena’s voice trembled. “You said that.”

“He wants to speak with you.”

“No.”

Daniel flinched as though she had slapped the table.

Mara put the phone on speaker. “Mrs. Reyes, he has not slept, and he is experiencing memories he believes are—”

“Lily,” Elena said.

The name seemed to travel through the room and settle on every surface.

Daniel leaned toward the phone. “Mom?”

A long pause followed. In the background, a faucet ran. Something clicked against a counter. Mara imagined Elena moving from room to room, looking for an exit in a house she had lived in for decades.

“You need to come home,” Elena said.

“I don’t know if I can.”

“You can.”

“There’s a girl here.”

“There is no girl.”

“Her name is Lily.”

“I know what you said her name is.”

Daniel looked at Mara. His expression was not angry yet. It was pleading, as though Mara might correct the conversation if she used the right words.

Elena continued, “You were an only child. You were born in Morristown. You lived with me and your father. We had Moth. We had the apartment. We had the white house in Parsippany for one year. That is all.”

“The yellow house,” Daniel said.

“There was no yellow house.”

“Mom, you sang to us there.”

“I sang to you.”

“To Lily.”

“I sang to you.”

Her certainty had an exhausted quality, as though she had been defending this fact against someone for years. Mara remembered Elena’s earlier admission: an unnamed girl who lived in the walls. She had not told Daniel about it. She wondered now whether Elena had been protecting him from an imaginary friend or from the possibility that an imaginary friend could become something else.

Daniel’s fingers tightened around the edge of the table. “Do you remember the storm?”

“No.”

“The basement window cracked.”

“No.”

“Dad tripped over my shoe.”

“Your father tripped over everything.”

For one second, Elena laughed. It was a genuine laugh, startled out of her. Daniel smiled in response. The sound made the room feel almost normal.

Then Elena said, “Who is with you?”

“Mara.”

“Is Lily there?”

Daniel’s face emptied.

Mara bent toward the phone. “Mrs. Reyes, you asked that before.”

“I did not.”

“You asked if Lily was in the recording.”

“I asked what he had seen.”

“You asked, ‘Is Lily in it?’”

The faucet stopped. For a moment the only sound was the hum of the laptop’s cooling fan.

Elena whispered, “Is she still there?”

Daniel stood so quickly that his chair struck the wall.

“Mom,” he said. “What does that mean?”

“Mara, turn off the call.”

“Where would she be?” Mara asked.

“Turn it off.”

“Was Lily ever—”

The camera came on.

Elena’s face appeared in the small rectangle, pale and wet-eyed. She was standing in a kitchen Mara had never seen, beside a refrigerator crowded with magnets. Behind her, a doorway opened onto a dark hall. The image stuttered. For one frame, a child’s hand seemed to be resting on Elena’s shoulder.

Elena looked over her shoulder.

Her mouth formed a word without sound.

Then the call ended.

Daniel remained standing. “She knows.”

“She may remember the imaginary girl,” Mara said.

“She knows Lily.”

“Your mother denied having a daughter.”

“She asked if Lily was still there.”

Mara had no answer that would not become evidence for him.

Daniel’s breathing quickened. “I need to go home.”

“You need to stay somewhere without a screen.”

“My apartment doesn’t have a television.”

“It has a phone.”

“I need my wallet.”

“You have your wallet.”

“My medication.”

“You don’t take medication.”

He looked toward the covered television. “There’s a card.”

“What card?”

“In my desk drawer. Mom sent it after my birthday. It says Danny and Lily.”

Mara felt the room contract around the sentence.

“Your mother sent you a birthday card addressed to both of you?”

“I didn’t know what it meant before.”

“Daniel.”

“I saw it last year. I thought it was a mistake. The envelope was already open.”

“Why didn’t you mention it?”

“Because I didn’t know Lily was missing.”

He said this with such calm conviction that Mara understood arguing would only make the card more necessary. If she refused to look, the object would remain in the category of forbidden proof, and forbidden proof had a way of acquiring weight.

She called the archive director, told him there had been a medical emergency, and asked for the county sedan. He objected until she said the words possible neurological event. Ten minutes later, Mara and Daniel stepped into the cold behind the building.

She took the tape key with her. The cassette stayed in the locked drawer. The old television remained covered, unplugged, and turned toward the wall.

Still, as they crossed the parking lot, Mara had the sensation that something was watching them leave.

Daniel’s apartment was on the second floor of a brick building near the river, twelve minutes from the archive. He apologized for the mess before opening the door. The apology was automatic and familiar. Mara had heard him make it when equipment deliveries arrived, when a co-worker borrowed a screwdriver, when he spilled coffee on a work order.

Inside were the ordinary markers of Daniel’s life: a folding table crowded with circuit boards, two plants dying in ceramic pots, a blue jacket over the back of a chair. A cat-shaped magnet clung to the refrigerator. Beneath it, in Elena’s handwriting, was a grocery list.

Moth, Mara thought.

Daniel went directly to the desk.

“Don’t touch anything until I see it,” Mara said.

He stopped with one hand on the drawer. “It’s mine.”

“I know.”

“And if the card is there?”

“Then we document it.”

“What if documenting it changes it?”

Mara looked at him. “That is what we’re trying to determine.”

The drawer contained receipts, loose batteries, a warranty for a toaster, and a stack of birthday cards tied with string. Daniel lifted the stack onto the desk. The top card showed a cartoon raccoon wearing a paper crown.

“Here,” he said.

The envelope underneath was white and unmarked. He turned it over. The flap had been opened and resealed with clear tape.

Mara put on nitrile gloves from the small emergency kit in her bag. She photographed the envelope with the county work phone, then stopped before pressing the shutter. A photograph was already too much to trust.

She opened the flap.

Inside was a folded card printed with blue balloons. On the front, in black ink, someone had written:

DANNY & LILY

The handwriting resembled Elena’s. Not exactly. The capital L leaned too far to the right, and the y in Lily had a long descending loop. But the pressure, the bluntness of the pen, the habit of crossing a t with a second stroke—all of it suggested a hand Mara had seen on Daniel’s emergency forms.

Daniel made a sound like a sob.

Mara unfolded the card.

Happy birthday to our two wonderful children.

The rest of the message had been obscured by a gray smear. Not ink. The paper itself seemed bruised. At the bottom was a date: June 17, 2014.

Daniel had turned twenty-one that year.

“Your mother sent this?” Mara asked.

“I told you.”

“Do you remember receiving it?”

“I remember opening it and thinking someone had made a cruel joke.”

“Who was the card addressed to when you first saw it?”

“Both of us.”

“And now?”

“Both of us.”

Mara looked again. The letters were clear. Danny and Lily. Two children. A shared birthday. A message written by a mother who had just denied that either the second child or the yellow house existed.

The apartment’s refrigerator clicked on.

Daniel turned toward the living room. “There’s a picture.”

“Stay here.”

“It’s by the door.”
