chapters.name: The Interview Schedule
chapters.content:
The alarm stopped after forty-three seconds.

Mara counted because counting was safer than listening. Two notes, a pause, two notes again. Behind Room Four’s closed door, Daniel had gone silent. The young laugh—if it had been a laugh—had vanished into the paper mill’s ordinary noises: a vent shuddering, a pipe knocking, the distant cough of a motor that had no reason to start.

Saira returned with a form on a metal clipboard.

“Response logged,” she said.

“What response?”

Saira looked at the blank lines. “Auditory vocalization. Duration forty-three seconds. Subject remained in room. No breach.”

“You don’t know whether it was Daniel.”

“We know the room was occupied by Daniel.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“It is what the form permits.”

Mara followed her back toward the briefing room. The corridor seemed longer than it had a minute before. She kept seeing the door’s narrow observation pane and Daniel’s moving mouth, though she had not been able to hear what he said. A person could be erased in a dozen administrative substitutions. Laugh became vocalization. Sister became kinship claim. Terror became noncompliance.

At the table, Dr. Vale had added a fourth stack of forms.

“This is the exposure protocol,” she said. “You are eligible to observe the first interview as a consultant.”

“Eligible, not invited.”

“You are invited under conditions.”

“Which conditions?”

“You will not bring your notebook. You will not ask Daniel whether Lily is real. You will not supply him with names, dates, locations, sensory prompts, or corrections. You will not contradict a report during collection. If you become distressed, you will raise your hand and leave.”

Mara glanced at the forms. “And if he asks me for help?”

“You will tell him that the interview is being conducted.”

“That isn’t help.”

“It is an answer.”

Vale turned the top page toward her. Across the heading ran a sequence of boxes.

EXPOSURE TIME: 00–06 HOURS.
EXPOSURE TIME: 06–24 HOURS.
EXPOSURE TIME: 24–72 HOURS.
EXPOSURE TIME: 30 DAYS.

“The first interview establishes onset and immediate content,” Vale said. “The second identifies persistence, elaboration, and conflict with verified biography. The third assesses consolidation. The thirty-day interview determines whether the material is fading, stabilizing, or propagating through relationships and records.”

“Propagating through records,” Mara said. “You mean the photograph.”

“We mean any external agreement with the subject’s account.”

“Daniel’s birthday card changed.”

“Possibly.”

“I saw it.”

“You saw an artifact during an active event. We have not authenticated its chain of alteration.”

Mara felt the old anger rise, familiar now as a pulse behind her eyes. “You seized it.”

“We contained it.”

“You can rename anything if you put it in a drawer.”

Vale ignored that. “Before the first interview, the subject is sedated. Not deeply. Enough to reduce agitation, prevent unauthorized movement, and limit the formation of an elaborated narrative during the interval between exposure and assessment.”

“Limit the formation?”

“Memory requires rehearsal. Rehearsal strengthens pathways.”

“Then you drug him so he can’t remember as well.”

“We sedate him so he cannot spend six hours teaching the anomaly to itself.”

The phrase stayed in the room.

Mara looked at Saira. “That’s what you think is happening?”

“We don’t know,” Saira said. “The protocol is built for the possibility.”

“What else is removed?”

“Personal objects. Clothing with family identifiers. Photographs. Letters. Phones. Wallets. Jewelry. Anything that can function as an anchor, prompt, or altered surface.”

“His mother’s photograph.”

“Yes.”

“His birthday card.”

“Yes.”

“You take away the evidence and then ask him what he remembers.”

“We ask what he reports,” Vale said. “Evidence is evaluated separately.”

Mara laughed once, without humor. “You’ve made a person into two filing systems.”

“The division protects both the person and the record.”

A nurse entered carrying a covered tray. She placed it on the side table and left without speaking. The smell of antiseptic drifted beneath the cover, sharp and medicinal. Mara thought of Daniel behind the door, sedated while Lily became more vivid in the dark.

“What happens at six hours?” she asked.

“Two interviewers, one clinical and one historical. Both pre-cutoff. No personal names beyond the subject’s assigned identifier. The subject is asked for the current date, place, age, and one verifiable fact. Then we ask what he believes occurred.”

“Not what he saw?”

“Seeing is already a contaminated verb.”

“What does he get to say?”

“Whatever he can say without prompting.”

“And you write it down.”

“Not verbatim.”

“Why not?”

Vale opened a drawer and removed a transparent evidence envelope. Inside lay a page of handwriting, folded twice. The writing was cramped and slanted, nearly filling every margin.

“This was recovered from a previous case,” she said. “Unauthorized notes.”

Mara did not touch the envelope. “What case?”

“Subject designation withheld.”

“Of course.”

“The employee heard a description from a technician and wrote down what she remembered. She had not viewed the source. She had not met the subject. Within forty-eight hours she was drawing floor plans of a house she had never visited.”

“A floor plan isn’t a memory.”

“She began sleeping in the hallway because the bedroom felt unsafe.”

Mara looked at the page. “What did the description say?”

“I will not repeat it.”

“Then how am I supposed to understand the risk?”

“You understand the result.”

“No. I understand that someone was frightened. That is not the same as understanding the mechanism.”

Vale returned the envelope to the drawer. “The mechanism is not a moral exemption.”

Mara stood. “You destroy every unauthorized copy?”

“Yes.”

“Transcripts?”

“Yes.”

“Sketches?”

“Yes.”

“Descriptive notes?”

“Yes.”

“Even if they’re made by affected subjects?”

“Especially then.”

“Because context may reconstruct the anomaly.”

Vale’s expression tightened. “You read the rule.”

“I’m asking whether you believe it.”

“I have watched a woman recognize her husband in a stranger because a nurse described the shape of a kitchen window. I have watched three staff members begin remembering the same nonexistent funeral after reading a compassionate account of a child’s grief. I believe context is a carrier.”

“And destroying those accounts prevents you from learning how it works.”

“Yes.”

The admission was so plain that Mara stopped.

Vale went on. “Containment is not research. Research is one of the activities containment sometimes permits when the risk can be bounded. We do not owe the anomaly a complete description of itself.”

“You owe the subjects a record.”

“We owe them care.”

“Care without testimony becomes custody.”

Saira shifted beside the table. She had been silent, but her fingers pressed against the edge of the clipboard.

Vale said, “You want to preserve Daniel’s words because you believe language gives him personhood.”

“I believe he has personhood before he speaks.”

“Then why make his speech into an artifact?”

“Because he may need someone to remember what happened to him.”

“He may need someone not to remember it.”

The covered tray seemed to breathe as the ventilation changed.

Mara thought of her father’s papers: receipts, letters, appointment cards, the evidence of a life that had narrowed around Ruth. She had wanted those records because they proved Elias had suffered. They did not prove Ruth existed. The distinction had seemed clean until Daniel said Lily’s name with the helpless certainty of a child calling from another room.

“Describe the thirty-day interview,” Mara said.

“By then the subject may have reorganized attachments. We test recognition of verified relatives, response to accurate photographs, orientation to personal history, and capacity to label the implanted material as constructed.”

“And if he can’t?”

“Then the case moves to long-term management.”

“Isolation?”

“Possibly.”

“Indefinitely?”

Vale did not answer immediately. “The schedule is not a promise of recovery.”

“It’s a schedule for deciding how long you keep him.”

“It is a schedule for deciding how much of the exposure remains active.”

“Those are the same thing when you’re the one behind the locked door.”

A knock came from the corridor. This time it was genuine. A young technician stood in the doorway, pale beneath the fluorescent lights.

“Dr. Vale,” he said. “The six-hour forms are ready.”

Vale nodded. “And the subject?”

“Sedated. Oriented to person and place before administration. He asked whether the girl could come in.”

Mara’s throat closed.

“What did you tell him?” Vale asked.

“That there was no girl.”

Vale’s gaze sharpened. “That was not an authorized response.”

The technician swallowed. “I’m sorry.”

“Do not correct subject content during collection. Record your own statement as an exposure risk. Saira, remove him from the wing and begin post-contact checks.”

The technician looked at Mara as if she might rescue him from the instruction. She could not. The border had already expanded to include a sentence.

Vale gathered the forms. “You may observe through the audio-free partition.”

“Audio-free?”

“You will see the interviewers and the subject. You will not hear the report.”

“Then I’ll learn nothing.”

“You will learn whether he can remain oriented.”

Mara followed them to the observation room. Through the glass, Daniel lay on a narrow bed with a blanket pulled to his chest. His eyes were closed. A nurse checked his pulse, then placed a numbered card on the table beside him. No photograph. No clock. No personal object at all.

On the other side of the partition, two interviewers entered. One carried a paper form. The other carried nothing.

Daniel opened his eyes.

Mara could not hear the questions, but she knew their shape. Name. Date. Place. Fact.

His lips moved. The first interviewer wrote. The second watched Daniel’s face.

Then Daniel began to cry.

Not dramatically. No struggle, no raised voice. Tears simply gathered and moved toward his ears while he stared at a blank wall. One interviewer reached for the covered tray and administered another measured dose.

Mara put her palm against the glass.

The wall remained blank. The room remained a room. Daniel’s grief crossed the partition without needing a picture.

Vale stood beside her. “This is why we restrict description.”

“His grief isn’t a description.”

“Not yet.”

Mara looked through the glass at the man who knew he had grown up in Newark and mourned a sister in Pennsylvania. She understood the department’s fear now—not as proof of its methods, but as the shape of the thing those methods had failed to contain. A memory could begin as an image, become a name, become a relationship, and finally ask the world to provide witnesses.

“What will you record?” she asked.

“Subject displays grief in response to an unverified kinship claim.”

“And what will you remember?”

Vale’s face gave nothing away.

Mara kept her hand against the glass until Daniel’s breathing evened and the interviewers lowered their pens.

“I’ll remember,” she said, “that he was crying.”

Vale turned toward her. “That may be enough.”

But it was not enough for Mara. In the corridor afterward, Saira gave her a fresh approved form and explained the schedule once more, this time as if reciting a liturgy. At twenty-four hours Daniel would be asked to repeat the account without being told what he had said at six. At seventy-two, the interviewers would compare not the story but its emotional pressure: which names produced fear, which facts produced relief, which invented rooms had acquired the authority of home. At thirty days, a clinician would place verified photographs before him one at a time and ask him to identify the people he had loved before the tape.

“Will he be allowed to keep anything?” Mara asked.

“Eventually.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the answer the schedule permits.”

Saira signed the form, then paused over the line marked PERSONAL OBJECTS WITHHELD. Her pen did not move.

“Do you ever write the names?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Not even for yourself?”

Saira looked toward Room Four. “Names are how a report becomes a person. That is also how it becomes portable.”

Mara took the form from her and read the final instruction: DESTROY ALL UNAUTHORIZED MATERIAL AFTER REVIEW. The words were stamped so deeply they had embossed the page beneath.

She thought of Daniel’s mother’s photograph locked somewhere below them, his phone and wallet sealed in numbered bags, the birthday card isolated as if paper could be guilty. She thought of Elias’s records, which had outlived the facts they were meant to preserve. Testimony could mislead. Silence could, too.

Behind the door, Daniel stirred. A nurse spoke to him, too softly for Mara to hear.

Mara did not write his grief down. She did not write Lily’s name. She did not make a sketch of the blank wall.

She stood outside the room and held the memory of his tears in the only place the department had not yet searched: not as evidence, not as a copy, but as a promise that a person could be more than the safe category assigned to him.

Vale watched her from the end of the corridor.

“Be careful,” she said.

Mara looked at the closed door. “That is what everyone keeps saying.”

“Yes.”

“And no one says what careful is for.”

Vale’s answer came after a long pause. “For the people who are still here.”

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: At the converted North Branch paper mill containment facility in rural Pennsylvania, Mara remains housed in a supervised consultant room above the former finishing floor under a wrist monitor. She has surrendered her coat, phone, keys, wallet, old incident notebook, and signing pen for controlled storage; she possesses department clothing and approved forms but did not bring her numbered notebook into Daniel’s first interview. Born March 4, 1985, she remains outside the primary vulnerability cohort but experiences emotional bleed-through, including grief for the nonexistent Ruth. She understands the formal exposure schedule of interviews at six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days, with sedation, isolation, removal of personal objects, and destruction of unauthorized descriptive material. She observed Daniel’s six-hour interview through an audio-free partition and was forbidden to prompt or correct him. Her goals remain to understand containment, protect Daniel, preserve the distinction between historical fact and emotional meaning, and resist procedures that reduce Daniel to a hazard. She now accepts that detailed testimony may itself transmit the anomaly but believes preserving a person’s grief and account is ethically necessary. She is physically stable but emotionally strained, angry, and increasingly distrustful of Dr. Vale’s secrecy.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: In Room Four of the paper mill’s supervised medical wing, Daniel remains isolated from outside clothing, wallet, phone, graduation photograph, birthday card, and ordinary family contact while undergoing the department’s scheduled exposure assessments. Born June 17, 1993, he can state verified facts about his Newark upbringing, Rutgers graduation, living mother Elena, and only-child status, but retains increasingly vivid memories of Lily, Pickle, the yellow house, and being loved there. Before his six-hour interview he was lightly sedated and oriented to person and place; during the interview he displayed quiet, intense grief in response to the unverified kinship claim. A young technician improperly told him that no girl existed, and the technician was removed for post-contact checks. Daniel distrusts the department and fears it will erase or discredit Lily; he has asked Mara to protect her name. He is physically stable but sedated, sleep-deprived, distressed, and emotionally divided between factual history and implanted childhood.

set.name: Saira Okafor
set.description: At the North Branch paper mill in rural Pennsylvania, Saira Okafor serves as operations historian and Mara’s orientation escort. Born October 12, 1978, she is outside the primary vulnerability cohort and has clearance to access the restricted vault gallery. She administers the formal AM-97-441 access rules and exposure documentation, including biometric, blood-oxygen, and spoken identity checks, remote analog playback restrictions, three-part signal severance, and the six-hour, twenty-four-hour, seventy-two-hour, and thirty-day interview schedule. She carries facility credentials and paper forms rather than relying on digital devices near the vault. She supervised Mara’s observation of Daniel’s six-hour interview and explained the removal of personal objects and destruction of unauthorized testimony. She is professional, guarded, and committed to distinguishing reported memories from verified facts, though Mara’s objections are exposing the ethical cost of that distinction. She remains responsible for escorting Mara and documenting facility responses.

set.name: Dr. Irena Vale
set.description: At the North Branch paper mill containment facility, Dr. Irena Vale oversees medical and procedural policy for AM-97-441. She is outside the primary vulnerability cohort and directs the birth-date cutoff, isolation and light sedation of exposed subjects, removal of personal objects, scheduled interviews, and destruction of unauthorized copies, transcripts, sketches, recordings, and descriptive notes. She believes emotionally detailed context can carry or reconstruct the anomaly and insists reports must be separated from facts even when they contain genuine grief. During Daniel’s six-hour assessment she enforced a no-prompt, no-correction protocol and removed a young technician who told Daniel that Lily did not exist, classifying the statement as an exposure risk. She remains composed, authoritative, and utilitarian, but Mara’s challenge that operational language can erase affected people has unsettled her. She denies subjects a vote in source-access decisions and continues to prioritize containment over preservation of testimony.

The department subjects Daniel to the formal six-hour exposure interview after light sedation and isolation from personal objects; he remains oriented to verified identity while grieving an unverified kinship claim.
Mara learns that unauthorized descriptions, transcripts, sketches, and recordings are destroyed because emotionally detailed context can induce secondary reconstruction in unexposed personnel.
A young technician improperly tells Daniel that no girl exists during interview preparation, and Dr. Vale removes him for post-contact checks after classifying the statement as an exposure risk.

Mara must review prior affected-subject testimonies under the department’s non-descriptive archive restrictions and confront how emotionally coherent false memories can be despite factual impossibility.

chapters.name: The Lakeside Camp
chapters.content:
The archive room had no windows, but someone had painted a thin blue line around the ceiling.

Mara noticed it only after Saira locked the door behind them. The line was the color of a summer sky seen through half-closed eyes, too pale to be cheerful and too deliberate to be merely institutional. Beneath it, four metal cabinets stood against the walls. Each drawer bore a designation, a date range, and a warning in black block letters: CONTENT REDACTED FOR SECONDARY TRANSMISSION RISK.

“Those are not the original files,” Saira said.

Mara glanced at her. “I didn’t ask.”

“You were looking at the cabinets as if they might be.”

“What happened to the originals?”

“Destroyed, if they contained descriptive material. Preserved, if they contained only administrative facts.”

“Who decides the difference?”

“Usually Dr. Vale. Sometimes a review panel.”

“And the panel is made up of people who haven’t seen the source?”

“People who have not been exposed to the source.”

Saira placed a paper folder on the table. It was gray, unmarked except for a red diagonal stripe and the designation AM-97-019. The pages inside had been cut with a ruler. Whole sentences ended in white gaps. In several places, black ink obscured not just a word but the line beneath it.

Mara pulled out the chair. “Why show me these?”

“Because you asked what came before Daniel.”

“I asked how you know the interview schedule works.”

“We don’t know that it works. We know what happened when we did not have one.”

Saira sat opposite her, keeping both hands visible on the table. The gesture looked procedural, but Mara had begun to understand that nothing at North Branch was only one thing. “This subject was born in 1992,” Saira said. “Female. Exposure occurred in a private residence after a family member purchased a used tape from an estate sale. The source was labeled with a summer date. The subject watched it alone.”

“Name?”

“Redacted.”

“Her name is not a visual detail.”

“It is a personal anchor. We use designations in the records.”

“You use designations when you speak to the people, too?”

“During collection.”

Mara opened the folder. The first page was a chronology stripped of everything except times, dosages, and locations.

SUBJECT LOCATED IN BEDROOM AT 21:14.

SUBJECT REMOVED FROM RESIDENCE AT 22:03.

SUBJECT REQUESTED RETURN TO LAKESIDE SITE AT 23:41.

There was no site address. The words lakeside site had been circled in pencil and then crossed out, as if even the category had become unsafe.

“What did she see?” Mara asked.

Saira’s mouth tightened. “You may read the testimony. Do not read aloud.”

“That seems designed to make me read aloud.”

“It is designed to make you responsible for your own mouth.”

The first testimony began halfway down the page.

SUBJECT: AM-97-019. AGE AT EXPOSURE: 31. DATE OF BIRTH: [REDACTED].

“I was at Camp Halcyon. The lake was low that year, and the dock had three loose boards. Grandma let me jump from the end even though she said the water was colder than it looked. She always said that. She wore the yellow visor when she was lying and the white visor when she meant it.”

A black rectangle covered the next three lines.

“Grandma had a laugh that started in her chest. If she was mad, she called me Margaret, but only when we were alone. In front of the others I was Birdie. That was the joke. I hated it until I didn’t.”

Mara stopped reading.

Across the table, Saira watched her. “What?”

“She says her grandmother called her Margaret.”

“That portion is not redacted.”

“Her birth certificate says Marjorie.”

Saira said nothing.

Mara returned to the page. The testimony continued in a different hand, perhaps written by an interviewer who had copied only permitted phrases.

“Rain came every afternoon at four. We played cards in the mess hall while the screens rattled. Grandma cheated at Old Maid by hiding the queen beneath her wrist. She said the camp rules did not apply to family.”

The next paragraph had been reduced to isolated sentences:

“She smelled like lake water and peppermint.”

“Her left knee hurt when storms came.”

“She knew the song about the fox.”

“I was not afraid when she was there.”

Mara felt the room tilt, though she remained seated. Daniel had described Pickle’s wet fur and the basement window. He had given Lily a chipped tooth and a hand that found his shoulder during thunder. The details were different, but the architecture was the same: a place assembled around an absence, furnished with the exact objects required to make longing feel inherited.

“Her grandmother died?” Mara asked.

“According to the subject, yes.”

“When?”

Saira turned to the administrative page. “The subject’s mother died when she was seven. Her maternal grandmother died in 1984. The subject was born in 1992.”

Mara looked again at the line about the yellow visor.

“Before she was born.”

“Eight years before.”

“Was the grandmother ever at Camp Halcyon?”

“There is no Camp Halcyon in the relevant county. There was a summer camp called Halcyon Pines in Maine, closed in 1976. The subject had never visited Maine. Her grandmother had never worked at a camp.”

“Then why keep the name?”

“Because the name mattered to her.”

“That is not an explanation.”

“It is the reason the file survived review.”

Saira slid a second page across the table. It was headed CLINICAL OBSERVATION—RESTRICTED. The language was colder, but the coldness could not fully conceal what it described.

The subject repeatedly attempted to leave the observation room. When redirected, she asked staff whether the road to the lake was open. She stated that her grandmother would be waiting at the dock and became distressed when informed that the facility was not near any lake. At 03:16 she said, “You can’t keep me from going home just because you don’t remember it.”

Mara read the sentence twice.

“Did she attack anyone?”

“No.”

“Did she damage anything?”

“No.”

“Then why was she restrained?”

“She tore the intravenous line out and tried to climb through a sealed window.”

“Because she wanted to go to a place that didn’t exist.”

“Because she believed someone she loved was waiting there.”

The distinction was precise enough to be useless.

Mara turned the page. The testimony grew more intimate as it went, though the most concrete descriptions had been removed. The woman remembered a boy at camp who had a scar shaped like a comma. She remembered stealing peaches from a kitchen crate and blaming a counselor named [REDACTED]. She remembered a private joke involving a dead moth, a canoe paddle, and the phrase “captain of the soup.” The interviewer had marked the phrase with a box and written SECONDARY CARRIER? in the margin.

“What does that mean?” Mara asked.

“During a follow-up interview, the clinician repeated the phrase to test recognition. Two nurses reported dreams about a dining hall afterward.”

“Because of three words?”

“Because of the emotional context attached to them.”

“What was the context?”

Saira’s eyes moved to the blacked-out lines. “We no longer know.”

“No longer know, or are not allowed to know?”

“Both.”

Mara leaned over the page without touching it. The redactions were not clean erasures. Beneath one, she could see the impression of handwriting pressed into the paper, a ghost of a sentence that had been cut away from the surviving copy. She imagined the missing words as a kind of pressure rather than language: wet wood, a storm coming, a grandmother’s hand closing around a wrist.

“Was she deprived as a child?” Mara asked.

Saira took a moment. “Her mother worked nights. Her father left when she was three. She spent long periods with an aunt who provided food and supervision. The records describe no abuse.”

“No abuse,” Mara repeated. “That’s the phrase people use when they mean a child survived.”

“The subject reported being lonely.”

“Before or after exposure?”

“Both. Before exposure, she described her childhood as ordinary and difficult to remember. After exposure, she described it as a waiting room.”

Mara thought of Daniel speaking about his real mother with embarrassment, as if Elena’s efforts were somehow humiliating beside the yellow house. A life did not have to be terrible to become vulnerable to replacement. It only had to contain an empty room.

Saira opened the third drawer and removed a narrow envelope. “There is an audio transcript,” she said. “Not a recording. The recording was destroyed.”

“Who transcribed it?”

“A pre-cutoff interviewer.”

“Then why is it safe?”

“It isn’t. It was reviewed, reduced, and approved for restricted reading.”

“That sounds like a confession.”

“It is a compromise.”

The transcript contained questions and answers, with entire exchanges replaced by brackets. The woman’s answers became longer near the end.

Q: What do you know about your grandmother’s death?

A: She died after the last summer. She was tired of being sick, but she didn’t want anyone to know. She made me promise not to tell my mother. I was nine.

Q: You were born in 1992. Your grandmother died in 1984.

A: That’s not right.

Q: We have records.

A: Records are what people leave when they don’t want to come with you.

Q: Do you understand that the camp may not have existed?

A: The camp existed for me.

Q: That is not the question.

A: It’s the only question you’re afraid of.

Mara lowered the page.

“Did she ever accept the dates?”

“Eventually, she could repeat them.”

“That isn’t acceptance.”

“No.”

“What happened to her?”

“She requested access to the source.”

“Of course she did.”

“She said she wanted to see the dock again.”

“Again?”

“She had not viewed the original a second time. But she remembered doing so.”

Mara felt a pressure behind her eyes. “And did you let her?”

“No.”

“Did she get better?”

Saira’s answer was almost inaudible. “She got more accurate.”

Mara waited.

“Over the next three weeks,” Saira continued, “she stopped insisting that the camp was physically accessible. She could identify her date of birth, her mother’s name, and the town where she lived. She acknowledged that her grandmother could not have known her as a child. But she continued to miss her. She asked whether missing someone made the person real in a different way.”

“What did the clinician say?”

“The response was not retained.”

“Destroyed?”

“Classified as interpretive language.”

Mara pushed the folder away. “You can’t even keep the answer.”

“We kept the subject’s question.”

“That’s supposed to comfort me?”

“No.” Saira looked tired now, older than the date on her personnel badge. “It is supposed to tell you what we are trying, badly, to protect.”

Mara stood and walked to the cabinet. The blue line around the ceiling continued behind it, unbroken. She imagined a lake on the other side of the wall: low water, loose boards, rain arriving each afternoon at four. The mind did not need a fixed film. It needed a weather system. Give it neglect and it would invent a grandmother. Give it loneliness and it would build a dock.

“Did the tape show the camp?” she asked.

“Not exactly.”

“Then what did it show?”

“A child near water. An older woman’s hand. A picnic table. A song without identifiable words.”

“That’s all?”

“That is all we can safely state.”

“And she made the rest.”

“The subject generated the autobiographical structure.”

“Because she wanted a grandmother.”

“Because the anomaly selected an emotionally available structure.”

Mara turned. “You say that as if the tape is a clinician.”

“No. A clinician might ask permission.”

The remark startled a laugh out of Mara. It was brief and unwelcome, but Saira’s expression softened in response.

On the table, the testimony waited with its black gaps and surviving fragments. Grandma. Birdie. Peppermint. The joke about soup. All of it impossible. None of it random.

Mara thought of her father claiming Ruth had stood beside him in a hallway. She had treated the claim as evidence of illness because illness was the only category available to her. Now she understood that factual impossibility did not make an experience emotionally incoherent. The tape did not hand its victims a single counterfeit childhood. It found the shape of what they had not received and populated it with weather, smells, nicknames, and private jokes.

The most frightening part was not that the woman had believed in a dead grandmother. It was that Mara could understand why.

“Why did she beg to return?” Mara asked.

Saira gathered the pages. “Because she knew it was false.”

Mara looked at her.

“She said the first time she wanted to go back, she believed the camp was real,” Saira said. “Later, she said she wanted to return even after she understood it was constructed. She told us the place was the only childhood she had ever been able to enter.”

“And you refused.”

“We refused the source.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Saira slid the papers into the folder. “We refused to make her choose between factual knowledge and emotional relief.”

“But you made the choice for her.”

“Yes.”

The honesty left no room for anger to land.

At the door, Saira stopped. “You are allowed to remember that she asked.”

“Am I?”

“You are not allowed to write the camp’s details down, repeat them, or reconstruct them from memory.”

Mara looked at the blue line circling the ceiling. “That’s a narrow permission.”

“It is the one we have.”

When they returned to the corridor, the paper mill smelled of dust, hot metal, and something faintly green. For one instant Mara thought of lake water warming beneath sunlight. She stopped walking.

Saira noticed. “What is it?”

“Nothing.”

The word felt dishonest. Nothing was what the records called an empty childhood, an absent sister, a father’s impossible daughter. Nothing was not empty. Nothing was where the anomaly put its hands.

At the end of the hall, Room Four remained sealed. Daniel was sleeping under observation, his personal objects locked away, Lily’s name absent from every approved form. Mara imagined asking him whether he would want the yellow house if he knew it had been built from loneliness. She imagined him answering that loneliness had built many real houses too.

She did not knock.

Instead, she returned to her consultant room and sat beneath the facility’s painted strip of sky. On the approved form, she wrote only the date, the file designation, and one sentence permitted by procedure:

SUBJECT RETAINED EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT TO A FACTUALLY IMPOSSIBLE LOCATION.

Mara stared at the sentence until the words lost their administrative shape.

Then, beneath it, without names or images or details, she added a second line.

THE ATTACHMENT WAS NOT EMPTY.

She knew the line would have to be submitted for review. She knew someone might black it out, classify it as interpretation, or order the page destroyed. Still, she left it there for the moment, a small act of witness beneath the painted sky.
