set.name: Peter Wirth
set.description: In the North Branch west-room medical area under pre-cutoff supervision, Peter remains agitated and emotionally defensive, with a bandaged hand and no personal possessions. Born November 9, 1994, he can state that his sister Rebecca lives in Ohio and that the concrete-room childhood is not factually verifiable, though he still cannot reliably picture Rebecca's face. He rejects the department's symbolic-integration language, demands acknowledgment that the constructed memory is part of his identity without calling it factual, and refuses consent for another interview. He remains separated from the relay and requires humane grounding and clinical care.

In the controlled inspection interviews, the lakeside-camp subject acknowledges that her grandmother associated with Camp Halcyon never lived, while choosing to retain her as a named internal story without making a factual claim.

The former foster-care subject rejects the belief that Helen Kessler stole him, but retains the constructed pantry memory as part of his identity and as a representation of wanting protection; he asks the record to distinguish his own change from departmental correction.
Alina Cho accepts that Owen Bell was not factually her schoolmate while insisting that the kindness she remembers remains an event in her own emotional life.

Peter Wirth refuses symbolic-integration language, demands that the department acknowledge the concrete-room memory as part of his identity without calling it factual, and declines consent for another interview.
Mara and Saira amend the rights ledger to distinguish factual status from subject meaning and to preserve subjects' own language about retained constructed memories.

chapters.name: Miri Again
chapters.content:
By the next morning, Owen Bell had learned three ways to ask for Dr. Vale.

The first was through the intercom, in a voice so calm that the orderly nearly answered without checking the panel. The second was by writing her name on the paper cup beside his bed. The third was by calling her Miri.

“Miri,” he said when Vale entered the observation room. “You came back.”

Vale stopped just inside the door.

The room had been stripped to its necessary objects: bed, drain, padded chair, wall clock, oxygen monitor, and a table bolted to the floor. No mirror. No window. No loose metal. Owen wore a gray facility shirt and drawstring trousers. His wrists were unrestrained, though the medication line remained taped to his left hand. A pre-cutoff nurse sat outside the open inner door, where she could see him without becoming part of the conversation.

Vale looked at the clock before looking at him. “State your name.”

“Owen Bell.”

“Date of birth.”

He gave it.

“Location.”

“North Branch medical wing.” He glanced at the wall. “Room Seven, although yesterday it was the upstairs room over the kitchen.”

“Yesterday was not upstairs.”

“I know.”

The answer was immediate. That was new.

Vale took the chair. She had not brought a file. Her hands were empty and visible, as the revised interview procedures required. She had argued for those procedures when they were still called emergency measures. Now Saira had begun calling them the first humane version of the protocol, and Vale had not corrected her.

Owen watched her settle. “Miri, you look older.”

“Dr. Vale.”

“That’s what you want me to call you.”

“That is my name.”

He smiled faintly. “No. Your name is Irena.”

Something moved behind Vale’s ribs. She kept her voice level. “Irena Vale is my name. Miri is a constructed identity associated with your exposure.”

“The girl in the shed wasn’t constructed.”

“The girl in the shed did not exist as you remember her.”

He looked down at his hands. “That isn’t the same sentence.”

“No,” Vale said. “It isn’t.”

She had spent thirty years making sentences narrower than that. She had used them to close doors, deny access, justify sedation, and explain to families why a person they loved could no longer be brought home. A thing was real or it was not. A memory was accurate or it was contaminated. The categories had kept her alive through the first incident, through Paul’s blank stare, through the years in which her brother could recognize the shape of her body but not the fact of having loved her.

The categories had also made it possible to call Owen a hazard before calling him a patient.

“Tell me about the shed,” she said.

Owen’s face changed. The room seemed to become less brightly lit, though the fixture remained steady.

“It was behind the orchard,” he said. “The door swelled in the rain. The hinge had copper wire wrapped around it because your father kept meaning to fix it. There was a green blanket in the loft and a red ribbon caught in the nail by the ladder.”

Vale felt each detail arrive with the force of an accusation. Swollen west door. Copper hinge. Blanket. Ribbon. The late-blooming tree that never gave enough fruit. Details she had not written anywhere accessible to Owen, details she had not spoken aloud since she was twelve.

“Continue,” she said, because stopping him too sharply might make the room dangerous.

“Miri and I hid there when Paul was angry. He’d stand outside and pretend he couldn’t find us. Sometimes he knew exactly where we were.” Owen rubbed his thumb against his palm. “She gave me half her sandwich. She told me not to cry because crying made him win.”

“There was no Miri in your childhood.”

His eyes flashed. “There was.”

“There was no girl named Miri who lived in that shed with you.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

Vale looked at him.

Owen leaned forward. The monitor registered a quickening pulse. “You keep asking if she was real. You never ask what she did.”

The nurse shifted outside the door. Vale raised one finger without turning. Not yet.

“What did she do?” Vale asked.

“She stayed.”

The word entered the room and did not need explanation.

Owen’s breathing became uneven. “She knew when to be quiet. She knew when to tell me the floorboards were holding. She knew the difference between hiding and being abandoned.” He swallowed. “She was the only person who knew how scared I was.”

Vale had heard versions of this from Daniel, from Alina, from the lakeside subject. She had entered each account as evidence of propagation. Emotional coherence increased risk. Sensory detail increased risk. The more a person suffered, the more carefully the department had isolated them.

But isolation had not prevented Owen from suffering. It had merely made the suffering occur where nobody had to call it by a human name.

“Miri is not me,” Vale said.

Owen stared at her.

“Not truly,” she continued. “The details you remember belong partly to my childhood, but the person you are describing is not Dr. Irena Vale.”

His mouth opened, then closed. “You finally understand.”

“I understand that you have separated the name from the person.”

“Miri isn’t you,” he said. “She’s me.”

Vale felt the statement as a physical disturbance, like a floor shifting under one foot.

Owen touched his chest. “She’s who I became in there. The boy who knew someone would stay. The boy who could be small and not get punished for it. I call you Miri because you stood where she stood, but you aren’t her.”

“And who is she?”

He looked toward the blank wall. For several seconds, his eyes followed something no one else could see.

“She’s the part of me that got out.”

The nurse came in then, not because Owen had lunged or shouted, but because his pulse had climbed beyond the agreed threshold. She checked the line and asked whether he wanted water. Owen said yes. Vale remained seated while the nurse poured it into the paper cup, careful not to touch the writing on its side.

MIRI.

Owen drank. When the nurse left, Vale said, “Do you believe I am Miri?”

“No.”

“Do you believe Miri was a factual person?”

“No.”

“Do you believe the apple shed existed?”

Owen closed his eyes. “Parts of it.”

“That is not a factual answer.”

“It’s the only honest one.”

Vale almost corrected him. The old reflex rose, precise and automatic: a place either existed or did not; a recollection either corresponded to an event or did not. But the shed had existed. Her family’s shed had existed, though not as Owen’s refuge. The anomaly had used real timber, real weather, real fear, and made from them an impossible childhood. Factual correction could separate the materials. It could not return them to an untouched arrangement.

“What do you want from me?” she asked.

Owen gave a tired laugh. “You’re the director. You tell people what they’re allowed to want.”

“I am asking you.”

He studied her. “Don’t cure me.”

Vale’s hands tightened on her knees.

“I don’t mean leave me like this,” he said. “I don’t want to wake up thinking you’re Miri. I don’t want to think I grew up in your shed. I want you to stop acting like taking those things away will make me Owen again.”

“Would you consent to continued supervision?”

“Do I get to say no?”

“Yes.”

“Then yes.” He looked at the cup. “For now.”

The interview ended at eleven minutes, though neither of them had called it an interview. Vale wrote the duration on the form afterward. She wrote that Bell retained present orientation, denied Vale’s factual identity as Miri, denied the literal existence of the remembered companion, and continued to experience the companion as emotionally protective.

Then she stopped.

The old form offered three classifications: resolved, unstable, or noncompliant.

She crossed out noncompliant.

She wrote: subject remains under supervision; factual distinction emerging; emotional attachment retained; no evidence of cure; no evidence of total loss.

The phrase looked inadequate. That was not the same as making it false.

At the records-room door, Mara was waiting with a pencil tucked behind one ear. Saira stood beside her, holding the access panel open.

“How did it go?” Mara asked.

Vale handed her the form.

Mara read it without speaking. “You called him subject.”

“He is a subject.”

“He is also Owen.”

Vale looked through the glass at the room. Owen had turned on his side, facing the wall. The nurse was checking the monitor without waking him.

“Yes,” Vale said. “He is also Owen.”

Saira took the form from Mara. “What changed?”

“His account.”

“No. What changed in you?”

Vale disliked the question because it was not procedural. She disliked it more because she knew the answer.

“I had been treating the distinction between true and false as if it were the distinction between person and hazard,” she said.

Mara’s expression did not soften. “That’s what the isolation order did.”

“I know.”

“You proposed indefinite neurological isolation.”

“I know.”

“You described it as necessary because ordinary rehabilitation was impossible.”

Vale looked down at the paper. “I still believe uncontrolled exposure is dangerous.”

“No one is asking you to believe otherwise.”

“They may never return to their prior identities.”

“Prior identities aren’t the only identities that deserve care.”

Vale had no immediate reply. In the corridor, the ventilation faltered for three seconds as the filters changed. Mara glanced at the clock, then at Saira, grounding herself in a measured event.

Vale said, “If we let every retained construction become a protected identity, we lose the distinction between acknowledgment and endorsement.”

“Then keep the distinction,” Saira said. “Do not keep the person out of the sentence.”

Through the glass, Owen stirred. His lips moved.

Mara stepped closer to the window but did not touch it. “What did he say?”

Vale listened through the intercom.

“Miri,” Owen murmured. “Don’t let him find us.”

The sentence belonged to the shed. It belonged to the boy. It belonged, Vale understood, to the moment before the boy learned that hiding could become a permanent address.

She entered the room again.

Owen opened his eyes. “You came back.”

“Yes.”

“Miri?”

“No,” Vale said. “Irena.”

He watched her, uncertain but awake.

“And Miri?”

Vale pulled the chair close enough that he would not have to raise his voice. “Miri is the name you gave to the part of you that learned protection was possible.”

His face crumpled, not with agreement but with exhaustion. “That sounds like something Saira would write.”

“It is not a factual diagnosis.”

“Good.”

“You may call that part Miri if you choose. You may not call me Miri without acknowledging that I am not her.”

A long silence followed.

“Can I call you Irena?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Can I still remember the shed?”

“Yes, with the distinction that it is not a verified part of your childhood.”

He considered this. “That’s a lot of words for a place that isn’t there.”

“It is,” Vale said. “But the words are yours to use.”

Owen turned his face toward the wall again. “Irena.”

“Yes?”

“Don’t make me say goodbye to her.”

Vale looked at the clock, the monitor, the sealed door, and the empty space where a childhood had been made from borrowed pieces. “I won’t,” she said. “But I will help you remember who she is.”

He did not answer. His breathing steadied by degrees.

Outside, Mara added a new line to the rights ledger: Bell rejects literal identity claim; retains chosen name for protective internal figure; requests continued care without forced erasure.

Vale read the line through the glass.

For years she had believed containment meant reducing the number of things that could happen. Now she saw another requirement, more difficult and less measurable: reducing the number of people who had to disappear in order for the institution to remain certain.

Owen slept. He was not cured. He was not wholly lost. Between those two failures of language, a person remained.

Vale stayed beside the bed until the nurse relieved her, and when Owen woke once more in the darkened room, she answered to Irena.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: In the North Branch supervised medical wing after the controlled interviews, Daniel remains physically exhausted but presently oriented, with no personal possessions. Born June 17, 1993, he can state his Newark upbringing, living mother Elena, Rutgers education, and current location. He identifies Lily as a constructed figure representing the person he invented so he would not be the only one who knew he was lonely, and says he loved her without treating her as a factual sister. He continues to need compassionate grounding and care.

set.name: Saira Okafor
set.description: In the North Branch source-isolated inspection and records rooms, Saira remains physically capable but fatigued, wearing monitored facility clothing with no possessions beyond the mechanical stopwatch and emergency cut controls. Born October 12, 1978, she conducts consent-based interviews and helps amend rights records so factual status is distinguished from subject meaning. She supports Bell’s continued humane supervision rather than forced erasure and remains separated from the relay while focused on ethical containment.

set.name: Dr. Irena Vale
set.description: In the North Branch medical wing and adjoining records corridor, Vale remains active, exhausted, and factually oriented as a pre-cutoff director born in 1969. During Bell’s supervised interview she learns that Miri is not truly Vale but a protective identity Bell formed within the constructed childhood. Shaken, she revises Bell’s classification away from noncompliant hazard language and accepts continued supervision without forced erasure, while still insisting that uncontrolled exposure is dangerous. She remains responsible for containment and is beginning to recognize that affected subjects require care as persons.

set.name: Owen Bell
set.description: In Room Seven of the North Branch supervised medical wing, Owen remains sedated intermittently but awake and medically monitored, with no personal possessions except a paper cup on which he wrote Miri. Born in 1993, he can state his verified identity, birth date, and location, and increasingly distinguishes Dr. Irena Vale from Miri. He describes the apple-shed childhood and Miri as a constructed, emotionally protective part of himself—the person he became in the only childhood where he felt protected—while retaining the memory without claiming it as factual. He consents to continued supervision for now, rejects forced erasure, and remains neither cured nor wholly lost.

During a supervised interview, Owen Bell distinguishes Dr. Irena Vale from Miri, identifying Miri as the protective part of himself formed by the constructed childhood; he accepts continued supervision without forced erasure while retaining the apple-shed memory as nonliteral and emotionally meaningful.

Dr. Vale revises Bell’s clinical classification from noncompliant to subject under supervision, documenting emerging factual distinction, retained emotional attachment, and neither cure nor total loss.

chapters.name: Lily's Name
chapters.content:
Daniel woke with the taste of copper in his mouth and a sentence already waiting for him.

Lily is not real.

The words had been written on the paper cup beside his bed. Not by a nurse. Not by Mara. His own handwriting, pressed so hard into the paper that the letters had broken its skin. Beneath them, in smaller script, he had added: This is not the same as saying she means nothing.

He stared at the cup until the room settled around it.

North Branch. Room Four, though the room had been moved twice during the breach and was now technically Room Four-B. Gray wall. Covered vent. A square of reinforced glass in the door. The narrow bed beneath him. His left wrist carrying the soft pressure of the monitor. No window, but a strip of morning-colored light beneath the door.

He named each thing aloud.

“My name is Daniel Reyes. June seventeenth, nineteen ninety-three. I’m in the North Branch medical wing. My mother is Elena Reyes. I went to Rutgers. The cup is paper.”

His voice sounded borrowed. He swallowed and tried again, adding the one fact Mara had taught him to keep when facts seemed too small to hold a life.

“My mother drove six hours to move me out of my first apartment.”

That one remained warm.

The latch opened. Mara entered with Saira behind her. Neither carried a file. Saira had the mechanical stopwatch clipped to the collar of her monitored shirt, and Mara held only a pencil and three sheets of paper. The pencil was not hers; all possessions in the wing belonged to the facility until the review board decided what could safely be returned. Daniel had started thinking of the pencil as Mara’s because it appeared whenever she came to ask him difficult questions.

“Good morning,” Mara said.

“Is it?”

“It is morning.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“No,” she said. “It wasn’t.”

Saira checked the monitor, then looked at him rather than at the numbers. “How present are you?”

“Present enough to be irritated.”

“That’s an encouraging sign.”

He almost smiled. The smile made something hurt behind his eyes.

Mara took the chair beside the bed. “You wrote something on the cup.”

“I know.”

“Do you want it removed?”

Daniel looked at the sentence. The black letters had begun to feather where the paper was damp from his hand. “No. I want to know if it’s allowed.”

“It’s your statement,” Mara said. “Not a description of the source. Not an instruction to anyone else. We can keep it in the rights ledger if you consent.”

“The rights ledger.”

“A record of what happened to you and what you say it means. Those are kept separately from factual findings.”

“Because meaning is contagious?”

“Because descriptions can be.”

“And this isn’t?”

Mara glanced at the cup. “It might be. We’ll assess it. But you made the distinction yourself. That matters.”

Daniel turned his face toward the blank wall. In the hospital-clean silence, Lily came back with impossible clarity: the angle of her shoulder, the chipped front tooth, the little impatient motion she made when he took too long to answer. Not the younger Lily from the footage. Not the older girl in the yellow room. Both, somehow, and neither.

“She’s here,” he said.

Mara did not ask who.

“Not in the room,” he added. “I know that. She’s in the way I know things.”

Saira pulled the stopwatch free but did not start it. “Can you describe what you know without describing her appearance?”

“Yes.” Daniel closed his eyes. “She’s the person I made when I was little and didn’t have anyone to tell me that being scared didn’t make me stupid. She knew when I was lying. She knew when I wanted my mother to ask me to stay. She was annoying.”

“Annoying?” Mara asked.

“She borrowed my things and never returned them. She sang the wrong words to songs. She could make me laugh when I was trying not to.”

“Are those memories factual?”

“No.”

The answer arrived quickly. It did not feel like a victory. It felt like stepping off a curb and discovering there was no street beneath him.

“No,” he repeated. “Not factual. But they’re mine.”

Mara wrote. The pencil moved without hurry.

Daniel watched her hand. “What happens when I leave?”

“We’re working on that.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the honest one.”

“My mother doesn’t know what to do with me.”

“She knows you’re ill.”

“I’m not ill in the way she means.”

“No,” Mara said. “You’re affected. That doesn’t mean you have no responsibility for what you do next.”

He sat up too quickly. The room tipped. Saira rose, but Daniel held up a hand until the dizziness passed.

“What I do next?” he said. “You mean if I tell her about Lily, I’m responsible for making her feel guilty?”

“I mean you can tell her what you experienced without accusing her of hiding a child.”

“She did hide things.”

“Everyone hides things.”

“Not a sister.”

“No,” Mara said gently. “Not a sister.”

The old anger flared, familiar as a reflex. It had once seemed directed at Mara, at the department, at Elena. Now he could see the shape beneath it: shame, turned outward because it was unbearable to leave it inside.

He swung his legs over the side of the bed. “I remember the apartment.”

Mara lowered the pencil. “Tell me about it.”

“The real one?”

“The one you identify as real.”

Daniel pressed his feet to the floor. The vinyl was cold. “Second floor. Newark. The radiator knocked all winter, even when it was off. The kitchen window didn’t close unless you lifted it first. There was a stain on the ceiling above my bed shaped like Florida.”

“Your mother lived there with you?”

“Yes. Just us.”

He had avoided this room in his mind for weeks. The apartment had been too ordinary to compete with the yellow house. Its rooms had no bright water, no Pickle asleep beneath the kitchen table, no Lily whispering from the hall. It held only thin walls and unpaid bills and Elena’s tired voice asking whether he had finished his homework.

But when he entered it now, it did not collapse.

“Elena worked mornings at the bakery,” he said. “She came home smelling like yeast and burnt sugar. On Saturdays she washed the sheets in the bathtub because the laundry room cost too much. She cut the crusts off my sandwiches until I was twelve, even though I told her I didn’t care.”

Mara’s expression remained still, but Daniel saw the grief move through it. Mara had learned not to interrupt grief just because it was factually authorized.

“She tried,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I hated that she tried.”

“That can also be true.”

“I hated the questions. Did you eat? Did you sleep? Did anybody bother you? She asked like she could inventory my life and fix the missing parts.”

“What were the missing parts?”

Daniel looked down at his hands. “Someone who knew me without asking. Someone who would notice if I left the room.”

“Your mother didn’t notice?”

“She noticed everything practical.” He rubbed his thumb over the paper cup. “She knew when my shoes were too small. She knew when I was pretending not to have a fever. She knew I wanted the blue backpack instead of the red one, even though I said the red one was fine.”

“And the rest?”

“The rest I didn’t tell her.”

His adolescent loneliness came back without the glamour Lily had given it. It was not a summer storm or a secret pact. It was eating cereal over the sink at midnight because he had missed dinner, sitting in the school bathroom while other boys shouted in the corridor, deleting messages before sending them because he could not bear to see anyone refuse him. It was the particular shame of needing comfort and believing that need proved he was defective.

He had built Lily in that space. Or the tape had found it. The difference mattered, but not enough to erase the result.

“When I was fourteen,” Daniel said, “I got a part-time job at a grocery store. My mother wanted me to save for college. I wanted to save for a car. Mostly I wanted to be somewhere she couldn’t check on me.”

“Did she check on you?”

“She called the store.”

“Why?”

“Because I told her I’d be home at ten and it was eleven.” He laughed once. “I thought it was humiliating. She said she was worried. I told her she was controlling. Then I hung up.”

“What happened when you got home?”

“She was asleep on the couch with the television on. There was a plate covered in foil on the table.”

“What was on it?”

“Chicken. Rice. The rice had gone hard.”

Mara wrote that down, then stopped.

Daniel felt the familiar impulse to make the story beautiful. To turn the cold rice into proof of an unspoken devotion, or into evidence that Elena had failed him. But the plate had only been a plate. His mother had been asleep because she had to work in the morning. She had left food because she expected him to come home hungry.

“I ate it,” he said. “I didn’t wake her.”

“Why not?”

“Because I was still angry.”

“And now?”

“I don’t know.”

Saira started the stopwatch. The click sounded very loud.

Daniel picked up the cup. “The strange thing is, Lily made all of that easier to hate. She gave me a witness. If she was there, then my loneliness was a fact shared by someone else. If she was my sister, then my mother’s failure wasn’t just failure to understand me. It was failure to protect both of us.”

Mara’s voice was quiet. “That is a powerful arrangement.”

“It is.”

“Does knowing it was constructed make the loneliness disappear?”

“No.”

“Does it make Elena innocent of everything?”

“No.”

“What does it change?”

Daniel looked at the words on the cup. Lily is not real.

“It gives me back the right to decide what happened,” he said. “Not the tape. Not the department. Not the version where my mother secretly had another child. But not the version where she was perfect either.”

Mara nodded. “That sounds like a difficult right.”

“It is.”

A knock came at the door. Three, two, three. Mara answered with the same pattern. Saira went to the observation panel and spoke with someone outside, then returned.

“Elena has agreed to a call,” she said. “Not today unless you want it. She asked whether you were still asking for Lily.”

Daniel’s throat closed.

“She remembers,” he said.

“She remembers you asking.”

“Did she say Lily’s name?”

Saira hesitated. “Yes.”

The name moved through him like a hand on his shoulder. For one second he was in the yellow room again, hearing rain against the glass, and Lily was beside him saying that Mara had arrived too late. Then the room became Room Four-B. The cup was paper. His mother was in New Jersey. The monitor pulsed green against his wrist.

“I want to call her,” he said.

Mara did not immediately approve it. “You can stop at any point. If either of you begins treating an unverified memory as evidence, we pause. No arguing about whether Lily existed.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Daniel considered the question. “I know Lily didn’t exist as my sister.”

“And what do you know about loving her?”

He looked toward the covered vent, where the air moved without making a sound.

“That part is mine,” he said.

The call was not made then. His pulse rose too quickly, and Saira ended the session before desire became another command. Daniel lay back, exhausted by the effort of being accurate.

At the door, Mara paused.

“Will you keep the cup?” she asked.

“Until the paper falls apart.”

“We can give you a fresh one and copy the statement.”

“No.” He held it carefully between both hands. “The handwriting matters.”

Mara accepted that. She left with Saira, and the door sealed.

Daniel remained alone with the two childhoods.

The apartment came first: the radiator, the Florida stain, Elena asleep beside the cold rice. Then the yellow house: sprinkler water flashing in the sun, Pickle’s brown back under the table, Lily’s chipped tooth and impatient song. One life had happened. The other had not. Neither could be made to carry the whole weight of him.

He lifted the cup and read the sentence again.

Lily is not real.

Below it, he added one more line.

I do not have to stop loving her.

Then, after a long while, he added her name once more—not as proof, not as a summons, but as an act of keeping.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: In the North Branch source-isolated medical-wing corridor and inspection area, Mara remains physically strained but factually oriented as a pre-cutoff consultant born March 4, 1985, wearing monitored facility clothing with no possessions except supervised paper, pencil, and gloves. She conducts Daniel’s consent-based grounding session, records his distinction between factual childhood and emotional meaning, preserves his own wording in the rights ledger, and supports a future carefully supervised call with Elena. She knows Daniel can reclaim his real upbringing without erasing Lily’s symbolic significance and remains determined to protect affected subjects’ rights while keeping AM-97-441 isolated.

set.name: Daniel Reyes
set.description: In Room Four-B of the North Branch supervised medical wing, Daniel remains physically exhausted but oriented, monitored, and without personal possessions except a paper cup on which he wrote that Lily is not real and that he does not have to stop loving her. Born June 17, 1993, he can state his Newark upbringing, living mother Elena, Rutgers education, and current location. He now recalls concrete details of the apartment and Elena’s imperfect but persistent care, recognizes his adolescent loneliness and shame without treating Lily as a factual sister, and understands Lily as a symbolic companion representing the family and witness he needed. He wants a future supervised call with Elena but postponed it after becoming distressed; he remains committed to retaining Lily’s emotional meaning without asserting her literal existence and requires compassionate grounding and care.

set.name: Elena Reyes
set.description: At her New Jersey home, Elena remains Daniel’s living mother and emergency contact, frightened and emotionally strained but protective. She knows Daniel is asking about Lily and has agreed in principle to a supervised call, including saying Lily’s name when asked, though the call has not yet occurred. She remains unaware of the Department’s full containment history and has not possessed the tape or altered artifacts. Her relationship with Daniel is tense because of his implanted memories, but she remains connected to his care and may hold unresolved knowledge about earlier anomalous effects.

set.name: Saira Okafor
set.description: In the North Branch supervised medical wing and adjoining source-isolated inspection area, Saira remains fatigued but physically capable, wearing monitored facility clothing with no possessions beyond the mechanical stopwatch and emergency cut controls. Born October 12, 1978, she monitors Daniel’s consent-based interview, checks his physical stability, enforces the distinction between unverifiable narrative and emotional meaning, and ends the session when his distress rises. She supports humane grounding, a future supervised Elena call, and continued care rather than forced erasure, while remaining separated from AM-97-441’s relay.

During a supervised session, Daniel recounts verifiable details of his Newark apartment and Elena’s practical care, recognizes that his adolescent loneliness was real without making Lily factual, and distinguishes Elena’s imperfect efforts from the constructed family narrative.

Daniel writes on a paper cup, “Lily is not real,” followed by “I do not have to stop loving her,” and consents in principle to a future call with Elena while postponing it after staff observe excessive emotional and physical strain.

chapters.name: A New Containment
chapters.content:
The first thing they did after the relay went dark was count the living.

Not the staff roster. Not the names on the emergency board, which had already acquired three contradictory versions of itself. They counted breathing bodies, one room at a time, beginning with the inspection corridor and moving outward through the paper mill’s medical wing.

“Thomas Keene,” Saira said.

“Here.”

“Alina Cho.”

“Here.”

Peter did not answer until the third attempt. When he did, his voice came from behind the observation glass, hoarse and furious.

“Here. I’m still here.”

Mara stood beside Saira with her gloved hands folded against her sternum. The corridor smelled of disinfectant, overheated copper, and the mineral damp that rose from the old paper mill’s foundations. Every light had been switched to the lowest permitted setting. The dark was no longer empty to anyone born after the cutoff. It had become a room they had once loved or feared.

Daniel was in Four-B. Owen was in Seven. Alina and Peter occupied the west rooms. Nia Bellweather remained under sedation in a sealed observation chamber, though she had never looked at the tape or the fragment. Vale had ordered a second medical sweep for anyone who had heard the intercom during the breach.

“Twenty-eight accounted for,” Saira said. “Four transferred to the lower ward. No unverified absences.”

“Say it without the word unverified,” Mara replied.

Saira looked at her, exhausted enough that the correction seemed almost cruel. Then she nodded.

“Twenty-eight accounted for. Four transferred. No one missing.”

Behind the next door, a young technician began to cry. He had spent the breach calling the mill his grandmother’s house. A pre-cutoff orderly sat with him and repeated his name, birth date, and the fact that the floor beneath him was concrete.

The source was not counted among the living.

It rested inside the suspension locker, still sealed in its canister, still capable of making the building remember what it had never been. The mechanical deck had stopped when Mara and Saira diverted its output into the localized inspection channel, but no one trusted the silence. Silence, where AM-97-441 was concerned, was only an unconfirmed condition.

Vale emerged from the vault gallery at 03:18, carrying the emergency authorization folder against her chest.

“Daniel has stabilized,” she said. “Bell is sedated. Cho and Wirth are conscious. We can proceed with burial at first light.”

“No,” Mara said.

Vale’s face had become an arrangement of fatigue and old anger. “The transfer was interrupted. The source activated the entire facility. We have documented secondary effects in personnel who never viewed the original medium. The only defensible action is to place it below the mill and seal the chamber permanently.”

“Permanently for the tape,” Saira said. “And for the people?”

Vale’s jaw tightened.

“The severely affected subjects remain in neurological isolation until they are no longer propagation risks.”

“There is no such endpoint in your memorandum,” Mara said. “There is only ‘until reassessment indicates acceptable stability.’”

“Then they remain until that assessment can be made.”

“By whom?”

“By the department.”

Mara thought of Daniel’s paper cup in Room Four-B. Lily is not real. I do not have to stop loving her. Two sentences written in a trembling hand, neither one surrendering to the other. The department’s forms had no place for that distinction. They had boxes for compliant, delusional, recovered, and dangerous. They had no box for a man who knew his sister was invented and still mourned the childhood she represented.

“You’re asking us to bury the source and the people,” Mara said.

“I’m asking us to stop the next breach.”

“Those are not the same thing.”

For several seconds, the only sound was the ventilation system cycling through its isolated loop. Somewhere below, a relay clicked once and failed to become anything else.

Saira opened the folder in Vale’s hands and removed the burial order. It was printed on heavy gray stock, with a red line across the top: SOURCE DISPOSITION—FINAL.

“Your order suspends all active reintegration work,” she said. “It also classifies testimony from exposed subjects as contaminated narrative. That language cannot stand.”

“It is contaminated narrative.”

“It is testimony,” Mara said.

Vale looked between them. “You think naming it differently changes what it does?”

“No,” Mara said. “I think naming it accurately changes what we do to the person who carries it.”

At 04:02, they convened the emergency review in the old sorting room. The room had once held bales of paper. Now it held a steel table, four pre-cutoff department officers, two legal observers, Saira, Mara, and Vale. No digital recorder was permitted. No photographs. The minutes would be written by hand, in deliberately non-descriptive language, and stored in a source-isolated archive after review.

The legal observers had been summoned from the department’s oversight office, not because anyone trusted oversight to arrive quickly, but because Mara had found the emergency number in an abandoned binder and called it three times until someone answered.

Vale presented the facts first. She did not describe the yellow house, the pool, the apple shed, or the voices. She used the approved vocabulary: individualized autobiographical construction, affective displacement, secondary narrative acquisition, source-linked propagation.

When she finished, Mara said, “You’ve described the hazard. You haven’t described the subjects.”

“The subjects are included in the hazard assessment.”

“They are not the assessment.”

The older legal observer, a woman named Judith Pell, turned a page in her notebook. “What remedy are you proposing?”

Mara had prepared the answer in the hours when the building had been pretending to be every place she had ever wanted to return to.

“First, no indefinite neurological isolation without a defined clinical purpose, review date, and subject consent where consent is possible. Second, every affected person receives an individual care plan: medical monitoring, psychological care, family counseling when safe, and an advocate independent of the containment team. Third, the person’s own statement is preserved, but only in a non-descriptive record that does not reproduce sensory or visual material. Fourth, factual status and emotional meaning are recorded in separate fields. One cannot be used to erase the other.”

Saira added, “And exposure interviews are voluntary after the immediate medical window. No one is compelled to produce meaning for our research.”

Vale stared at the table. “If they refuse, we lose clinical information.”

“If they refuse,” Saira said, “we learn that they have a right to refuse.”

The discussion lasted two hours. Vale argued that consent was compromised by the anomaly itself. Mara agreed that exposure could distort judgment, but pointed out that the department had treated every later decision as permanently invalid, even after subjects demonstrated factual orientation. Saira proposed staged consent: immediate stabilization under emergency authority, followed by repeated plain-language explanations and renewed permission at each intervention.

Judith Pell asked whether the new framework would allow subjects to retain false memories.

“No,” Vale said.

“Yes,” Mara said.

The contradiction hung over the table.

Mara continued. “It allows them to retain their own internal experiences without requiring the department to certify them as history. We do not have to say Lily existed. We do have to acknowledge that Daniel’s love exists. We do not have to say Owen spent a summer in an orchard with Miri. We do have to acknowledge that the protective identity he formed is part of the condition we are treating.”

“And if acknowledgment strengthens it?” Vale asked.

“Then we monitor that possibility. We don’t solve the danger by pretending a person has no interior life.”

At 06:41, the review issued an interim ruling. Vale’s burial order was suspended. The ninety-day renewable isolation authorized before the crisis was replaced with a thirty-day clinical review period, renewable only with written justification, subject notification, and independent oversight. Daniel, Owen, Alina, Peter, and the other affected subjects would remain source-separated, but not abandoned. Their rooms would no longer be called isolation cells in the records. They became supervised care rooms.

The language felt small. Mara knew small changes could still be doors.

By 08:00, the vault team began resealing AM-97-441.

The procedure had been rewritten while they waited. No single person would handle the canister. No exposed or vulnerable personnel could enter the gallery. The source would remain in the suspension locker, but the locker itself would be placed inside a second ceramic housing with an independent ground and a mechanical status indicator. The vault’s service corridor would be physically separated from the medical wing. No intercom, emergency speaker, alarm panel, or building cable would share a conduit with it.

They removed the deck from the room without powering it on. It was wrapped in untreated ceramic cloth and placed in a sealed transport coffin for later disposition under observation. The tape was not played. No one attempted to inspect the reels. No one spoke about what it might show.

Mara watched through the gallery glass as two pre-cutoff handlers lifted the canister into the new housing. Saira stood at the control station with three cut switches beneath her palms. Vale occupied the third position.

“Source status?” Saira asked.

“Contained,” said Handler One.

“Signal status?”

“Absent.”

“Authority to close?”

A pause.

Vale looked through the glass at Mara. There was something unguarded in her expression—not agreement, exactly, but recognition of the cost of the old certainty.

“Close,” Vale said.

The housing door sealed. The suspension locker descended six inches and locked. No laughter came through the walls. No child pressed a hand against the glass. The vault remained a vault.

Mara exhaled only after the final mechanical indicator turned from amber to black.

In the afternoon, she and Saira carried the new rights ledger to the medical wing. It was a thick paper volume, its pages numbered by hand. The first section listed facts that could be independently verified: names, dates of birth, present location, known medical needs. The second section was headed SUBJECT-OWNED MEANING. Beneath it, the subject could dictate a sentence, refuse a sentence, amend a sentence, or leave the page blank.

Daniel was awake when they entered. He looked at the ledger, then at Mara.

“Is that where you write that I’m better?”

“No,” Mara said. “It’s where you decide what we’re allowed to say about you.”

He considered this. “Can I write that Lily isn’t real?”

“You can.”

“And that I love her?”

“You can write that too.”

He pulled the ledger closer. His hand shook, but less than it had in the morning. He dictated while Saira wrote, preserving his wording without adding interpretation.

Daniel Reyes states that Lily is not a factual sister. Daniel Reyes states that Lily remains emotionally significant. Daniel Reyes does not consent to any record describing Lily’s appearance, voice, location, or events as factual. Daniel Reyes requests assistance rebuilding contact with his mother when medically appropriate.

He read the entry twice.

“Is that enough?” he asked.

“It’s yours,” Saira said. “It doesn’t have to be enough for us.”

In Room Seven, Owen added a similar limitation concerning Miri. Alina asked that the record preserve the fact that she had felt kindness, without naming the person who had never been her classmate. Peter refused to dictate anything and signed only the refusal line. The ledger preserved that too.

No copies were made. The original remained in the source-isolated records room. Summaries for oversight used only the non-descriptive vocabulary and omitted the subjects’ sensory narratives. There would be no training film, no public case study, no redacted exhibit circulated among officials who wanted to understand the phenomenon from a safe distance. Understanding would not be permitted to become another route of distribution.

That evening, Mara stood at the end of the corridor while Saira checked on the rooms. The paper mill was quiet. Not peaceful. Peace implied an ending. This was maintenance: doors checked, names repeated, consent renewed, the source kept apart from every system that could carry it.

“Do you think this is containment?” Saira asked when she returned.

Mara looked toward the sealed vault, though no part of it was visible from there.

“It is containment of the source,” she said. “For the people, it has to be care.”

Saira nodded. “And if care fails?”

“Then we revise it. We don’t turn failure into a sentence.”

Behind Room Four-B’s glass, Daniel slept with one hand closed around the paper cup. The words on it had begun to fade from handling, but Mara could still read them.

Lily is not real.

I do not have to stop loving her.

The department had once believed safety required choosing one sentence and destroying the other. The new containment began by refusing that choice. Facts would remain facts. Feelings would remain feelings. Neither would be allowed to impersonate the other, and neither would be surrendered merely because the distinction was difficult to maintain.

In the records corridor, Saira locked the ledger away.

In the vault, the cassette waited without light.

And for the first time since Mara had bought it for three dollars, the tape was not moving toward anyone.

set.description: In Room Four-B of the North Branch supervised medical wing, Daniel remains physically exhausted but oriented and monitored, born June 17, 1993. He has no personal possessions except the paper cup bearing his statement that Lily is not real and that he does not have to stop loving her; his wording is also preserved in the source-isolated rights ledger.
